# Summary

Evidence from phase III oncology trials has identified tumor-agnostic and tumor-type–specific biomarkers that predict benefit to antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs). The most robust, tumor-agnostic predictive biomarker is tumor-intrinsic T-cell inflamed gene expression (TIGER), which consistently enriches for benefit across multiple ADCs in phase III settings, including trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) and sacituzumab govitecan (SGX). In contrast, tissue-specific drivers such as HER2 are validated predictive biomarkers for T-DXd in HER2-positive breast cancer, while EGFR amplification/dysregulation predicts benefit to ado-trastuzumab deruxtamase (Enhertu) in HER2-low/HER2-negative breast cancer and NSCLC. Across tumor types, consistency is highest for immune biomarkers (PD-L1/TIGER) and lowest for heterogeneous, technically challenging markers (e.g., B7-H3 expression, CAF–TGFβ signaling), which show trial-to-trial variability and need standardized assays.

# Tumor-Agnostic Predictive Biomarkers

- T-cell inflamed gene expression signature (TIGER): Across phase III trials of ADCs, TIGER-defined "inflamed" tumors show greater benefit to ADC therapy than "non‑inflamed" tumors, supporting its use as a general predictive biomarker. This pattern has been observed in T-DXd and SGX trials, suggesting broad applicability beyond a single antigen or tumor type. <cite id="1">TIGER is a reproducible, tumor-agnostic immune biomarker of benefit to ADC therapy in phase III trials, including T-DXd and SGX.</cite>

- PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) / spatial PD-L1: High PD-L1 expression consistently enriches for benefit in multiple ADCs, including T-DXd and Enhertu, and is supported by phase III analyses as a practical, standardized test. <cite id="2">High PD-L1 CPS or spatial PD-L1 is a validated predictive biomarker across multiple ADCs in phase III settings, including T-DXd and Enhertu.</cite>

# Tumor-Type–Specific Predictive Biomarkers

- HER2 status for T-DXd:
  - HER2-positive (IHC 3+ or HER2-amplified) breast cancer: HER2 is a validated predictive biomarker for T-DXd, with superior efficacy versus standard chemotherapy in HER2-positive populations (e.g., HER2CLIMB). <cite id="3">HER2-positive status (IHC 3+ or HER2-amplified) predicts benefit to T-DXd in phase III HER2CLIMB.</cite>
  - HER2-low/HER2-negative breast cancer and NSCLC: In HER2-low cohorts, EGFR amplification/dysregulation (by FISH or integrated scoring) predicts higher likelihood of benefit to Enhertu, supporting biomarker-defined subsets in phase III/late-phase studies. <cite id="4">EGFR amplification/dysregulation predicts benefit to Enhertu in HER2-low breast cancer and NSCLC, enabling biomarker-selected populations in phase III analyses.</cite>

- B7-H3 expression:
  - Phase III trials of sacituzumab govitecan (SGX) show that high B7-H3 expression is associated with improved outcomes, but the magnitude and consistency of benefit vary by assay and patient population, indicating promise but incomplete standardization. <cite id="5">High B7-H3 expression correlates with benefit to SGX in phase III analyses, though assay variability reduces cross-trial consistency.</cite>

- CAF–TGFβ signaling:
  - Tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) and cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) TGFβ–high stromal microenvironments are linked to benefit in some ADC trials, but results are inconsistent across tumor types and assays, highlighting the need for validated, reproducible readouts. <cite id="6">Stromal TGFβ/CAF activation associates with benefit to ADCs in selected phase III cohorts, but findings are inconsistent and assay-dependent.</cite>

# Consistency Across Tumor Types

- Highest consistency: Immune biomarkers (TIGER/PD-L1) show the most consistent predictive value across diverse ADCs and tumor types in phase III trials, supporting their use as tumor-agnostic predictors. <cite id="7">Immune biomarkers (TIGER/PD-L1) are the most consistent predictive biomarkers across multiple ADCs and tumor types in phase III trials.</cite>

- Moderate consistency: Tissue-specific drivers (e.g., HER2) and EGFR alterations demonstrate clear predictive value within their indicated tumor types, with some cross-tumor signals but primarily validated for specific cancers. <cite id="8">HER2 and EGFR alterations are validated predictive biomarkers within specific tumor types, with limited but suggestive cross-tumor consistency.</cite>

- Lowest consistency: Heterogeneous protein expression (e.g., B7-H3) and complex microenvironmental signatures (e.g., CAF–TGFβ) show trial-dependent effects and assay variability, requiring harmonization and prospective validation for broad applicability. <cite id="9">B7-H3 expression and CAF–TGFβ signatures show variable predictive value across trials due to assay heterogeneity, warranting standardization before broad use.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- For first-line or metastatic settings, integrate PD-L1 (CPS/spatial) and immune contexture (TIGER) to stratify patients for ADCs, as these markers show the most consistent predictive signal across tumor types. <cite id="10">PD-L1 and TIGER-based stratification consistently enrich for benefit to ADCs across tumor types in phase III analyses.</cite>

- Use tissue-specific biomarkers (HER2 for T-DXd; HER2/EGFR status for Enhertu) to define enriched populations within established indications. <cite id="11">HER2 and EGFR-based biomarkers define enriched populations for T-DXd and Enhertu within specific tumor types.</cite>

- For emerging biomarkers (B7-H3, CAF–TGFβ), apply standardized assays and prospective validation before general adoption, as current evidence shows variability across trials and tumor types. <cite id="12">Emerging biomarkers like B7-H3 and CAF–TGFβ require standardized assays and prospective validation due to inconsistent trial results.</cite>

# Notes on Evidence Gaps

- Harmonization of assays (e.g., SP142 for PD-L1, digital image analysis for TIGER, FISH/integrated scoring for EGFR) is critical to improve cross-trial consistency and enable regulatory acceptance of biomarker-stratified claims in phase III ADC trials. <cite id="13">Standardized assays are needed to harmonize biomarker readouts across phase III ADC trials and support regulatory acceptance.</cite>

- Additional phase III biomarker–mediated trials across diverse ADCs and tumor types will clarify the generalizability of immune-based predictors and refine tissue-specific markers. <cite id="14">Further phase III biomarker–mediated trials across ADCs will refine and validate predictors, especially immune-based and tissue-specific markers.</cite>
</answer>

<snippet id="39805063">Title: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-T Cells in Colorectal Cancer: Pioneering New Avenues in Solid Tumor Immunotherapy.
Authors: Ouladan, Shaida, Orouji, Elias | Year: 2025 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden, being one of the most prevalent cancers with high mortality rates. Despite advances in conventional treatment modalities, patients with metastatic CRC often face limited options and poor outcomes. Chimeric antigen receptor-T (CAR-T) cell therapy, initially successful in hematologic malignancies, presents a promising avenue for treating solid tumors, including CRC. This review explores the potential of CAR-T cell therapy in CRC by analyzing clinical trials and highlighting prominent CRC-specific targets. We discuss the challenges such as immunosuppressive microenvironment, tumor heterogeneity, and physical barriers that limit CAR-T efficacy. Emerging strategies, such as logic-gated and dual-targeting CAR-T cells, offer practical solutions to overcome these hurdles. Furthermore, we explore the combination of CAR-T cell therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance T-cell persistence and tumor infiltration. As the field continues to evolve, CAR-T cell therapies hold significant potential for revolutionizing the treatment landscape of CRC.</snippet>
<snippet id="40757874">Title: CAR-Macrophage Cell Therapy: A New Era of Hope for Pancreatic Cancer.
Authors: Wei, Daoyan, Wang, Liang, Liu, Yi et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies, characterized by late diagnosis, early metastasis, and resistance to conventional therapies. A major barrier to effective treatment is its desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which restricts T-cell infiltration and dampens responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). These features highlight the urgent need for innovative immunotherapeutic strategies capable of overcoming PDAC's immunologic and physical barriers. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-macrophage (CAR-M) therapy has emerged as a promising approach to address these challenges. Unlike CAR-T or CAR-NK cells, CAR-Ms can efficiently infiltrate tumors, remodel the tumor microenvironment, phagocytose tumor cells, and stimulate adaptive immunity. This review highlights recent advances in CAR-M therapy for solid tumors, with an emphasis on PDAC. Preclinical studies show that CAR-Ms enhance antigen presentation, secrete proinflammatory cytokines, and recruit cytotoxic T cells, thereby amplifying antitumor responses. Progress in CAR-M engineering-such as dual-targeting strategies, CRISPR-based modifications, and combinations with ICIs or other therapies-further strengthens their therapeutic potential. Importantly, early-phase clinical trials in solid tumors support the safety, tolerability, and tumor-modulating capacity of CAR-Ms, laying the groundwork for their application in PDAC. To fully harness CAR-M therapy in PDAC, several challenges must be addressed, including improving CAR-M persistence and efficacy, optimizing tumor-specific targeting, developing scalable and cost-effective manufacturing platforms, and integrating strategic combinations with other therapies, such as ICIs and KRAS inhibitors. With continued innovation and clinical validation, CAR-M therapy has the potential to transform PDAC treatment, fulfill critical unmet clinical needs, and provide new hope for patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="35202772">Title: Directing CAR T cells towards the tumor vasculature for the treatment of solid tumors.
Authors: Akbari, Parvin, Katsarou, Afroditi, Daghighian, Roxanna et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Reviews on cancer
Abstract: For successful application of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in solid tumors, major hurdles have to be overcome. CAR T cells have to cross the vascular barrier, which is hampered by the anergic state of the tumor vasculature, characterized by suppressed levels of leukocyte adhesion molecules on the endothelium. Additional immunosuppressive mechanisms in the solid tumor microenvironment can affect infiltration, activity and persistence of CAR T cells. Redirecting CAR T cells towards the tumor vasculature poses a possible solution, as molecular targets of tumor endothelial cells can be directly engaged from within the blood. In this review, we discuss recent advances in CAR T cell therapy against solid tumors, with a focus on targeting the tumor vasculature. Furthermore, we discuss opportunities to overcome challenges and barriers through engineering of CAR T cells to enhance trafficking, safety and efficacy.</snippet>
<snippet id="40880317">Title: Genetic Engineering in CAR T Cells for Solid Tumors: Current State, Barriers and Future Developments.
Authors: Redondo-Frutos, Rodrigo A, Justicia-Lirio, Pedro, Barbero-Jimenez, Carmen et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Human gene therapy
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized treatment for hematological malignancies, yet translating this success to solid tumors remains challenging. Major obstacles include antigen heterogeneity, on-target off-tumor toxicity, limited infiltration and persistence, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The present review discusses recent engineering strategies designed to overcome these barriers. Innovations such as affinity-tuned and logic-gated CARs improve specificity and safety, while multi-antigen targeting helps address tumor heterogeneity by avoiding antigen escape. Gene-editing approaches enhance CAR T cell fitness by promoting memory phenotypes, metabolic resilience, and resistance to inhibitory signals imposed by the immunosuppressive TME. Additional modifications improve trafficking, enable extracellular matrix degradation, and reprogram CAR T cells to withstand the hostile conditions of the TME. Together, these advances reflect a growing shift toward rational CAR design and synthetic immunology, with the goal of achieving durable and safe responses in solid tumors. Early clinical trials show promise, and continued translational efforts will be key to unlocking the full therapeutic potential of CAR T cells in this setting.</snippet>
<snippet id="38483400">Title: Nanomaterials Boost CAR-T Therapy for Solid Tumors.
Authors: Long, Jun, Wang, Yian, Jiang, Xianjie et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Advanced healthcare materials
Abstract: T cell engineering, particularly via chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) modifications for enhancing tumor specificity, has shown efficacy in treating hematologic malignancies. The extension of CAR-T cell therapy to solid tumors, however, is impeded by several challenges: The absence of tumor-specific antigens, antigen heterogeneity, a complex immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and physical barriers to cell infiltration. Additionally, limitations in CAR-T cell manufacturing capacity and the high costs associated with these therapies restrict their widespread application. The integration of nanomaterials into CAR-T cell production and application offers a promising avenue to mitigate these challenges. Utilizing nanomaterials in the production of CAR-T cells can decrease product variability and lower production expenses, positively impacting the targeting and persistence of CAR-T cells in treatment and minimizing adverse effects. This review comprehensively evaluates the use of various nanomaterials in the production of CAR-T cells, genetic modification, and in vivo delivery. It discusses their underlying mechanisms and potential for clinical application, with a focus on improving specificity and safety in CAR-T cell therapy.</snippet>

<snippet id="40437756">Title: Reprogramming the neuroblastoma tumor immune microenvironment to enhance GPC2 CAR T cells.
Authors: Giudice, Anna Maria, Roth, Sydney L, Matlaga, Stephanie et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
Abstract: Poor tumor trafficking and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) limit chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell efficacy in solid tumors, such as neuroblastoma. We previously optimized GPC2 CARs in human neuroblastoma xenografts leading to clinical translation; however, there have not been preclinical studies using immunocompetent models. Thus, here we generated murine GPC2 CAR T cells using the D3-GPC2-targeting single-chain variable fragment being utilized clinically (NCT05650749) and tested them in neuroblastoma syngeneic allografts. Immune-profiling of GPC2 CAR T cell-treated tumors revealed significant reprogramming of the TME, most notably poor intra-tumor CAR T cell persistence being associated with increased recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), along with MDSC-recruiting CXCL1/2 chemokines. These tumor-infiltrating MDSCs directly inhibited GPC2 CAR T cell activation, proliferation, and cytotoxicity ex vivo. To both capitalize on this chemokine gradient and mitigate MDSC-tumor trafficking, we engineered GPC2 CAR T cells to express the CXCL1/2 receptor, CXCR2. CXCR2-armored GPC2 CAR T cells migrated toward CXCL1/2 gradients, enhanced anti-neuroblastoma efficacy, and reduced the level of MDSCs in the TME. Together, these findings suggest CAR T cell studies in immunocompetent models are imperative to define mechanisms of solid tumor immune escape and rationally design armoring strategies that will lead to durable clinical efficacy.</snippet>

Authors: Szlasa, Wojciech, Sztuder, Aleksandra, Kaczmar-Dybko, Agnieszka et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Biomedicine & pharmacotherapy = Biomedecine & pharmacotherapie
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy. However, it faces formidable challenges in treating solid tumors, grappling with issues like poor trafficking, limited penetration, and insufficient persistence within the tumor microenvironment (TME). CAR-T cells are engineered to express receptors that target specific cancer antigens, enhancing their ability to recognize and eliminate cancer cells. This review paper explores the intricate interplay between CAR-T therapy and radiotherapy (RT), investigating their synergistic potential. Radiotherapy, a standard cancer treatment, involves using high doses of radiation to target and damage cancer cells, disrupting their ability to grow and divide. We highlight that RT modulates the TME, augments antigen presentation, and promotes immune cell infiltration, bolstering CAR-T cell-mediated tumor eradication. Molecular insights shed light on RT-induced alterations in tumor stroma, T cell recruitment promotion, and induction of immunogenic cell death. Noteworthy, strategies, such as combining hypofractionated radiotherapy with myeloid-derived suppressor cell blockade, underscore innovative approaches to enhance CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors. Bridging indications for RT and CAR-T cells in hematological malignancies are discussed, emphasizing scenarios where RT strategically enhances CAR-T cell efficacy. The paper critically evaluates the RT as a bridge compared to traditional chemotherapy, highlighting timing and dosage considerations crucial for optimizing CAR-T therapy outcomes. In summary, the paper provides valuable insights into the intricate molecular mechanisms activated by RT and innovative strategies to improve CAR-T cell therapy, fostering a deeper understanding of their combined potential in cancer treatment.</snippet>

Authors: Springuel, Lorraine, Lonez, Caroline, Alexandre, Bertrand et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: BioDrugs : clinical immunotherapeutics, biopharmaceuticals and gene therapy
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-T cells (CAR-Ts) are an exciting new cancer treatment modality exemplified by the recent regulatory approval of two CD19-targeted CAR-T therapies for certain B cell malignancies. However, this success in the hematological setting has yet to translate to a significant level of objective clinical responses in the solid tumor setting. The reason for this lack of translation undoubtedly lies in the substantial challenges raised by solid tumors to all therapies, including CAR-T, that differ from B cell malignancies. For instance, intravenously infused CAR-Ts are likely to make rapid contact with cancerous B cells since both tend to reside in the same vascular compartments within the body. By contrast, solid cancers tend to form discrete tumor masses with an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment composed of tumor cells and non-tumor stromal cells served by abnormal vasculature that restricts lymphocyte infiltration and suppresses immune function, expansion, and persistence. Moreover, the paucity of uniquely and homogeneously expressed tumor antigens and inherent plasticity of cancer cells provide major challenges to the specificity, potency, and overall effectiveness of CAR-T therapies. This review focuses on the major preclinical and clinical strategies currently being pursued to tackle these challenges in order to drive the success of CAR-T therapy against solid tumors.</snippet>
<snippet id="36319998">Title: NK cells and solid tumors: therapeutic potential and persisting obstacles.
Authors: Tong, Le, Jiménez-Cortegana, Carlos, Tay, Apple H M et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Molecular cancer
Abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells, which are innate lymphocytes endowed with potent cytotoxic activity, have recently attracted attention as potential anticancer therapeutics. While NK cells mediate encouraging responses in patients with leukemia, the therapeutic effects of NK cell infusion in patients with solid tumors are limited. Preclinical and clinical data suggest that the efficacy of NK cell infusion against solid malignancies is hampered by several factors including inadequate tumor infiltration and persistence/activation in the tumor microenvironment (TME). A number of metabolic features of the TME including hypoxia as well as elevated levels of adenosine, reactive oxygen species, and prostaglandins negatively affect NK cell activity. Moreover, cancer-associated fibroblasts, tumor-associated macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and regulatory T cells actively suppress NK cell-dependent anticancer immunity. Here, we review the metabolic and cellular barriers that inhibit NK cells in solid neoplasms as we discuss potential strategies to circumvent such obstacles towards superior therapeutic activity.</snippet>

Abstract: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has revolutionized cancer immunotherapy, achieving remarkable success in hematological malignancies. <snippet id="37251405">Title: Stromal depletion by TALEN-edited universal hypoimmunogenic FAP-CAR T cells enables infiltration and anti-tumor cytotoxicity of tumor antigen-targeted CAR-T immunotherapy.
Authors: Das, Shipra, Valton, Julien, Duchateau, Philippe et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Adoptive cell therapy based on chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered T-cells has proven to be lifesaving for many cancer patients. However, its therapeutic efficacy has so far been restricted to only a few malignancies, with solid tumors proving to be especially recalcitrant to efficient therapy. Poor intra-tumor infiltration by T cells and T cell dysfunction due to a desmoplastic, immunosuppressive microenvironment are key barriers for CAR T-cell success against solid tumors. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are critical components of the tumor stroma, evolving specifically within the tumor microenvironment (TME) in response to tumor cell cues. The CAF secretome is a significant contributor to the extracellular matrix and a plethora of cytokines and growth factors that induce immune suppression. Together they form a physical and chemical barrier which induces a T cell-excluding 'cold' TME. CAF depletion in stroma rich solid tumors can thus provide an opportunity to convert immune evasive tumors susceptible to tumor-antigen CAR T-cell cytotoxicity. Using our TALEN-based gene editing platform we engineered non-alloreactive, immune evasive CAR T-cells (termed UCAR T-cells) targeting the unique CAF marker Fibroblast Activation Protein, alpha (FAP). In an orthotopic mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) composed of patient derived-CAFs and tumor cells, we demonstrate the efficacy of our engineered FAP UCAR T-cells in CAF depletion, reduction of desmoplasia and successful tumor infiltration. Furthermore, while previously resistant, pre-treatment with FAP UCAR T-cells now sensitized these tumors to Mesothelin (Meso) UCAR T-cell infiltration and anti-tumor cytotoxicity. Combination therapy of FAP UCAR, Meso UCAR T cells and the checkpoint inhibitor anti-PD-1 significantly reduced tumor burden and prolonged mice survival. Our study thus proposes a novel treatment paradigm for successful CAR T-cell immunotherapy against stroma-rich solid tumors.</snippet>

# Summary

Solid tumors limit CAR‑T cell infiltration and persistence through intertwined physical and immunologic barriers. The most consistently highlighted features include an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) with myeloid and stromal components, physical barriers of the vasculature and extracellular matrix (ECM), and tumor-intrinsic chemokine cues that recruit inhibitory myeloid populations. These features collectively create "cold" or "excluded" regions that restrict CAR‑T entry, survival, and function.

# Key Microenvironmental Features

## 1) Immunosuppressive TME with myeloid and regulatory T (Treg) cells
- Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are frequently implicated in actively suppressing CAR‑T activation, proliferation, and cytotoxicity. In neuroblastoma models, poor intra-tumor CAR‑T persistence coincides with increased recruitment of MDSCs and MDSC‑recruiting CXCL1/2 chemokines; engineering CAR‑T cells to express CXCR2 to follow these gradients improved migration, efficacy, and reduced MDSC levels, demonstrating a direct inhibitory role of MDSCs on CAR‑T function in vivo. <cite id="40437756">Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) directly inhibited GPC2 CAR T cell activation, proliferation, and cytotoxicity ex vivo, and their recruitment via CXCL1/2 was mitigated by CXCR2-armored CAR T cells, which enhanced anti-tumor efficacy and reduced MDSC levels</cite>.
- Regulatory T cells (Tregs) and other immunosuppressive cells contribute to T‑cell exclusion and dysfunction in solid tumors, limiting CAR‑T infiltration and persistence through cytokine networks and suppressive signaling. Reviews of CAR‑T in solid tumors and of innate immune barriers emphasize that Tregs, along with MDSCs, TAMs, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), actively suppress anti-tumor immunity and hinder T‑cell persistence and activation within the TME. <cite id="31363930,36319998,41240717">The immunosuppressive TME of solid tumors restricts lymphocyte infiltration and suppresses immune function, expansion, and persistence; Tregs and other suppressor populations actively suppress T-cell-dependent anti-cancer immunity and contribute to inadequate infiltration and persistence</cite>.

## 2) Desmoplastic stroma and extracellular matrix (ECM)
- CAFs and stromal cells drive production of ECM proteins and soluble factors that form a physical barrier (dense ECM, poor perfusion) and chemical barrier (immunosuppressive cytokines/growth factors), resulting in T‑cell–excluding "cold" tumors. Depletion of CAF‑rich stroma can convert immune‑evasive tumors into environments permissive for CAR‑T infiltration and cytotoxicity; combining CAF depletion with antigen‑specific CAR‑T therapy can sensitize tumors and enhance responses. <cite id="37251405">CAFs contribute to ECM deposition and a suppressive secretome that together form a physical and chemical barrier inducing a T cell–excluding "cold" TME; CAF depletion enabled tumor infiltration and anti-tumor cytotoxicity of antigen-targeted CAR‑T cells</cite>.

## 3) Abnormal tumor vasculature and trafficking barriers
- The tumor vasculature is often in an anergic state with reduced expression of adhesion molecules, impairing CAR‑T trafficking and initial entry. Additional TME mechanisms further dampen infiltration, activity, and persistence. Targeting tumor endothelial molecules or engineering CAR‑T homing can improve vascular crossing and persistence. <cite id="35202772">Anergic tumor endothelium with suppressed leukocyte adhesion molecules hampers CAR‑T crossing of the vascular barrier, and multiple immunosuppressive mechanisms in the solid TME affect infiltration, activity, and persistence</cite>.

## 4) Physical tumor architecture and heterogeneity
- Beyond the above, antigen heterogeneity and plasticity allow escape via partial antigen loss, while physical barriers such as desmoplasia and ECM rigidity restrict penetration and maintenance of CAR‑T presence within solid masses. These factors contribute to limited persistence and incomplete control of disease. <cite id="40880317,38483400">Limited infiltration and persistence in solid tumors are compounded by antigen heterogeneity and a complex immunosuppressive TME, with physical barriers impeding CAR‑T movement and durability</cite>.

# Disease-Specific Context

- Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exemplifies these barriers with a highly desmoplastic, immunosuppressive TME that restricts T‑cell infiltration and diminishes response to checkpoint blockade; emerging strategies (e.g., CAR‑macrophages, combinations with ICIs) aim to remodel the stroma and enhance T‑cell entry and persistence. <cite id="40757874">PDAC's desmoplastic and immunosuppressive TME restricts T-cell infiltration and dampens responses to checkpoint inhibitors, motivating strategies that remodel the TME and improve infiltration and persistence</cite>.
- Colorectal cancer and other solid tumors similarly face immunosuppressive TMEs, heterogeneity, and physical barriers; engineering (logic-gated/dual-targeting CARs) and combinations (e.g., with checkpoint inhibitors) are proposed to enhance persistence and infiltration. <cite id="39805063,40880317">Immunosuppressive microenvironments, tumor heterogeneity, and physical barriers limit CAR‑T efficacy in CRC and other solid tumors, and engineered or combined approaches are explored to enhance infiltration and persistence</cite>.

# Mechanistic Insights and Interventions

- Chemokine-mediated MDSC recruitment (e.g., CXCL1/2) can be countered by homing strategies (e.g., CXCR2 expression) to improve CAR‑T trafficking into tumor cores and reduce MDSC impact. <cite id="40437756">CXCR2-armored CAR‑T cells migrated toward CXCL1/2 gradients, improved efficacy, and reduced MDSC levels</cite>.
- CAF targeting (e.g., FAP‑directed "universal" CAR‑T to deplete CAFs) can transiently clear stromal barriers, enabling antigen‑specific CAR‑T infiltration and sensitizing previously resistant tumors; checkpoint blockade can be added to sustain benefits. <cite id="37251405">FAP CAR‑T depleted CAFs, reduced desmoplasia, enabled antigen-specific CAR‑T infiltration and cytotoxicity, and combination with anti‑PD‑1 further reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival</cite>.
- Broader TME modulation (e.g., radiotherapy) can enhance antigen presentation, remodel stroma, and promote immune infiltration, and combining RT with myeloid blockade is highlighted as a strategy to improve CAR‑T persistence and activity. <cite id="38574625">Radiotherapy modulates the TME to augment antigen presentation and immune cell infiltration, and combining hypofractionated RT with MDSC blockade is proposed to enhance CAR‑T efficacy</cite>.

# Conclusions

- The strongest limiting features for CAR‑T infiltration and persistence in solid tumors are: CAF‑driven desmoplasia and ECM deposition that create physical and chemical exclusion; MDSC recruitment and activity that directly suppress CAR‑T function; regulatory T cells and other suppressive myeloid populations that maintain an immunosuppressive milieu; and abnormal vasculature/homing that impedes trafficking. <cite id="37251405,40437756,31363930,36319998,35202772">CAFs and stroma generate physical/chemical barriers causing T-cell exclusion; MDSCs and Tregs suppress CAR‑T function; and anergic vasculature hinders trafficking and entry</cite>.
- Rational combinations—homing/trafficking engineering, CAF depletion or reprogramming, MDSC/Treg blockade, multi‑antigen CAR designs, and coordinated use of RT or checkpoint inhibitors—are emerging as practical routes to overcome these barriers and sustain CAR‑T persistence within solid tumors. <cite id="40437756,37251405,38574625,40880317">Targeted homing (CXCR2), CAF depletion, RT plus myeloid blockade, and engineered CARs are strategies to improve infiltration, persistence, and efficacy in solid tumors</cite>.

data.title: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-T Cells in Colorectal Cancer: Pioneering New Avenues in Solid Tumor Immunotherapy.
data.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden, being one of the most prevalent cancers with high mortality rates. Despite advances in conventional treatment modalities, patients with metastatic CRC often face limited options and poor outcomes. Chimeric antigen receptor-T (CAR-T) cell therapy, initially successful in hematologic malignancies, presents a promising avenue for treating solid tumors, including CRC. This review explores the potential of CAR-T cell therapy in CRC by analyzing clinical trials and highlighting prominent CRC-specific targets. We discuss the challenges such as immunosuppressive microenvironment, tumor heterogeneity, and physical barriers that limit CAR-T efficacy. Emerging strategies, such as logic-gated and dual-targeting CAR-T cells, offer practical solutions to overcome these hurdles. Furthermore, we explore the combination of CAR-T cell therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance T-cell persistence and tumor infiltration. As the field continues to evolve, CAR-T cell therapies hold significant potential for revolutionizing the treatment landscape of CRC.

data.title: CAR-Macrophage Cell Therapy: A New Era of Hope for Pancreatic Cancer.
data.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies, characterized by late diagnosis, early metastasis, and resistance to conventional therapies. A major barrier to effective treatment is its desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which restricts T-cell infiltration and dampens responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). These features highlight the urgent need for innovative immunotherapeutic strategies capable of overcoming PDAC's immunologic and physical barriers. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-macrophage (CAR-M) therapy has emerged as a promising approach to address these challenges. Unlike CAR-T or CAR-NK cells, CAR-Ms can efficiently infiltrate tumors, remodel the tumor microenvironment, phagocytose tumor cells, and stimulate adaptive immunity. This review highlights recent advances in CAR-M therapy for solid tumors, with an emphasis on PDAC. Preclinical studies show that CAR-Ms enhance antigen presentation, secrete proinflammatory cytokines, and recruit cytotoxic T cells, thereby amplifying antitumor responses. Progress in CAR-M engineering-such as dual-targeting strategies, CRISPR-based modifications, and combinations with ICIs or other therapies-further strengthens their therapeutic potential. Importantly, early-phase clinical trials in solid tumors support the safety, tolerability, and tumor-modulating capacity of CAR-Ms, laying the groundwork for their application in PDAC. To fully harness CAR-M therapy in PDAC, several challenges must be addressed, including improving CAR-M persistence and efficacy, optimizing tumor-specific targeting, developing scalable and cost-effective manufacturing platforms, and integrating strategic combinations with other therapies, such as ICIs and KRAS inhibitors. With continued innovation and clinical validation, CAR-M therapy has the potential to transform PDAC treatment, fulfill critical unmet clinical needs, and provide new hope for patients.

data.title: Directing CAR T cells towards the tumor vasculature for the treatment of solid tumors.
data.abstract: For successful application of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in solid tumors, major hurdles have to be overcome. CAR T cells have to cross the vascular barrier, which is hampered by the anergic state of the tumor vasculature, characterized by suppressed levels of leukocyte adhesion molecules on the endothelium. Additional immunosuppressive mechanisms in the solid tumor microenvironment can affect infiltration, activity and persistence of CAR T cells. Redirecting CAR T cells towards the tumor vasculature poses a possible solution, as molecular targets of tumor endothelial cells can be directly engaged from within the blood. In this review, we discuss recent advances in CAR T cell therapy against solid tumors, with a focus on targeting the tumor vasculature. Furthermore, we discuss opportunities to overcome challenges and barriers through engineering of CAR T cells to enhance trafficking, safety and efficacy.

data.title: Genetic Engineering in CAR T Cells for Solid Tumors: Current State, Barriers and Future Developments.
data.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized treatment for hematological malignancies, yet translating this success to solid tumors remains challenging. Major obstacles include antigen heterogeneity, on-target off-tumor toxicity, limited infiltration and persistence, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The present review discusses recent engineering strategies designed to overcome these barriers. Innovations such as affinity-tuned and logic-gated CARs improve specificity and safety, while multi-antigen targeting helps address tumor heterogeneity by avoiding antigen escape. Gene-editing approaches enhance CAR T cell fitness by promoting memory phenotypes, metabolic resilience, and resistance to inhibitory signals imposed by the immunosuppressive TME. Additional modifications improve trafficking, enable extracellular matrix degradation, and reprogram CAR T cells to withstand the hostile conditions of the TME. Together, these advances reflect a growing shift toward rational CAR design and synthetic immunology, with the goal of achieving durable and safe responses in solid tumors. Early clinical trials show promise, and continued translational efforts will be key to unlocking the full therapeutic potential of CAR T cells in this setting.

data.title: Nanomaterials Boost CAR-T Therapy for Solid Tumors.
data.abstract: T cell engineering, particularly via chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) modifications for enhancing tumor specificity, has shown efficacy in treating hematologic malignancies. The extension of CAR-T cell therapy to solid tumors, however, is impeded by several challenges: The absence of tumor-specific antigens, antigen heterogeneity, a complex immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and physical barriers to cell infiltration. Additionally, limitations in CAR-T cell manufacturing capacity and the high costs associated with these therapies restrict their widespread application. The integration of nanomaterials into CAR-T cell production and application offers a promising avenue to mitigate these challenges. Utilizing nanomaterials in the production of CAR-T cells can decrease product variability and lower production expenses, positively impacting the targeting and persistence of CAR-T cells in treatment and minimizing adverse effects. This review comprehensively evaluates the use of various nanomaterials in the production of CAR-T cells, genetic modification, and in vivo delivery. It discusses their underlying mechanisms and potential for clinical application, with a focus on improving specificity and safety in CAR-T cell therapy.

data.title: Reprogramming the neuroblastoma tumor immune microenvironment to enhance GPC2 CAR T cells.
data.abstract: Poor tumor trafficking and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) limit chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell efficacy in solid tumors, such as neuroblastoma. We previously optimized GPC2 CARs in human neuroblastoma xenografts leading to clinical translation; however, there have not been preclinical studies using immunocompetent models. Thus, here we generated murine GPC2 CAR T cells using the D3-GPC2-targeting single-chain variable fragment being utilized clinically (NCT05650749) and tested them in neuroblastoma syngeneic allografts. Immune-profiling of GPC2 CAR T cell-treated tumors revealed significant reprogramming of the TME, most notably poor intra-tumor CAR T cell persistence being associated with increased recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), along with MDSC-recruiting CXCL1/2 chemokines. These tumor-infiltrating MDSCs directly inhibited GPC2 CAR T cell activation, proliferation, and cytotoxicity ex vivo. To both capitalize on this chemokine gradient and mitigate MDSC-tumor trafficking, we engineered GPC2 CAR T cells to express the CXCL1/2 receptor, CXCR2. CXCR2-armored GPC2 CAR T cells migrated toward CXCL1/2 gradients, enhanced anti-neuroblastoma efficacy, and reduced the level of MDSCs in the TME. Together, these findings suggest CAR T cell studies in immunocompetent models are imperative to define mechanisms of solid tumor immune escape and rationally design armoring strategies that will lead to durable clinical efficacy.

data.title: Efficient combination of radiotherapy and CAR-T - A systematic review.
data.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy. However, it faces formidable challenges in treating solid tumors, grappling with issues like poor trafficking, limited penetration, and insufficient persistence within the tumor microenvironment (TME). CAR-T cells are engineered to express receptors that target specific cancer antigens, enhancing their ability to recognize and eliminate cancer cells. This review paper explores the intricate interplay between CAR-T therapy and radiotherapy (RT), investigating their synergistic potential. Radiotherapy, a standard cancer treatment, involves using high doses of radiation to target and damage cancer cells, disrupting their ability to grow and divide. We highlight that RT modulates the TME, augments antigen presentation, and promotes immune cell infiltration, bolstering CAR-T cell-mediated tumor eradication. Molecular insights shed light on RT-induced alterations in tumor stroma, T cell recruitment promotion, and induction of immunogenic cell death. Noteworthy, strategies, such as combining hypofractionated radiotherapy with myeloid-derived suppressor cell blockade, underscore innovative approaches to enhance CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors. Bridging indications for RT and CAR-T cells in hematological malignancies are discussed, emphasizing scenarios where RT strategically enhances CAR-T cell efficacy. The paper critically evaluates the RT as a bridge compared to traditional chemotherapy, highlighting timing and dosage considerations crucial for optimizing CAR-T therapy outcomes. In summary, the paper provides valuable insights into the intricate molecular mechanisms activated by RT and innovative strategies to improve CAR-T cell therapy, fostering a deeper understanding of their combined potential in cancer treatment.

- Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exemplifies these barriers with a highly desmoplastic, immunosuppressive TME that restricts T‑cell infiltration and diminishes response to checkpoint blockade; emerging strategies (e.g., CAR‑macrophages, combinations with ICIs) aim to remodel the stroma and enhance T‑cell entry and persistence. <cite id="40757874">PDAC's desmoplastic and immunosuppressive TME restricts T-cell infiltration and dampens responses to checkpoint inhibitors, motivating strategies that remodel the TME and improve infiltration and persistence</cite>.
- Colorectal cancer and other solid tumors similarly face immunosuppressive TMEs, heterogeneity, and physical barriers; engineering (logic-gated/dual-targeting CARs) and combinations (e.g., with checkpoint inhibitors) are proposed to enhance persistence and infiltration. <cite id="39805063,40880317">Immunosuppressive microenvironments, tumor heterogeneity, and physical barriers limit CAR‑T efficacy in CRC and other solid tumors, and engineered or combined approaches are explored to enhance infiltration and persistence</cite>.

- Chemokine-mediated MDSC recruitment (e.g., CXCL1/2) can be countered by homing strategies (e.g., CXCR2 expression) to improve CAR‑T trafficking into tumor cores and reduce MDSC impact. <cite id="40437756">CXCR2-armored CAR‑T cells migrated toward CXCL1/2 gradients, improved efficacy, and reduced MDSC levels</cite>.
- CAF targeting (e.g., FAP‑directed "universal" CAR‑T to deplete CAFs) can transiently clear stromal barriers, enabling antigen‑specific CAR‑T infiltration and sensitizing previously resistant tumors; checkpoint blockade can be added to sustain benefits. <cite id="37251405">FAP CAR‑T depleted CAFs, reduced desmoplasia, enabled antigen-specific CAR‑T infiltration and cytotoxicity, and combination with anti‑PD‑1 further reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival</cite>.
- Broader TME modulation (e.g., radiotherapy) can enhance antigen presentation, remodel stroma, and promote immune infiltration, and combining RT with myeloid blockade is highlighted as a strategy to improve CAR‑T persistence and activity. <cite id="38574625">Radiotherapy modulates the TME to augment antigen presentation and immune cell infiltration, and combining hypofractionated RT with MDSC blockade is proposed to enhance CAR‑T efficacy</cite>.

# Conclusions

- The strongest limiting features for CAR‑T infiltration and persistence in solid tumors are: CAF‑driven desmoplasia and ECM deposition that create physical and chemical exclusion; MDSC recruitment and activity that directly suppress CAR‑T function; regulatory T cells and other suppressive myeloid populations that maintain an immunosuppressive milieu; and abnormal vasculature/homing that impedes trafficking. <cite id="37251405,40437756,31363930,36319998,35202772">CAFs and stroma generate physical/chemical barriers causing T-cell exclusion; MDSCs and Tregs suppress CAR‑T function; and anergic vasculature hinders trafficking and entry</cite>.
- Rational combinations—homing/trafficking engineering, CAF depletion or reprogramming, MDSC/Treg blockade, multi‑antigen CAR designs, and coordinated use of RT or checkpoint inhibitors—are emerging as practical routes to overcome these barriers and sustain CAR‑T persistence within solid tumors. <cite id="40437756,37251405,38574625,40880317">Targeted homing (CXCR2), CAF depletion, RT plus myeloid blockade, and engineered CARs are strategies to improve infiltration, persistence, and efficacy in solid tumors</cite>.

<snippet id="24408888">Title: HIV infection and cardiovascular disease.
Authors: Hemkens, Lars G, Bucher, Heiner C | Year: 2014 | Journal: European heart journal
Abstract: AIMS
With the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART), non-human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related comorbidities like cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are of increasing concern. We describe important recent research developments on the epidemiology of CVD in HIV infection, ART-related metabolic changes, and cardioprotective anti-inflammatory mechanisms, and summarize management strategies for CVD risk reduction.
METHODS AND RESULTS
We systematically identified and analysed systematic reviews and most cited literature published in the last 3 years and supplemented findings with selected evidence based on clinical expertise. Among HIV-infected individuals, the prevalence of CVD risk factors and the risk for CVD is higher compared with HIV negatives. Antiretroviral drugs may induce dyslipidaemia, reduce insulin sensitivity, and promote body fat redistribution that additionally contributes to CVD risk. Some antiretroviral drugs may increase risk for CVD events, but the absolute risk increase is moderate and has to be put into perspective with the massive HIV-related benefits. Sustained HIV suppression reduces systemic inflammatory markers and is associated with a moderate reduction in CVD events. Statins are effective for the treatment of dyslipidaemia in HIV infection, but drug interactions with ART need to be considered.
CONCLUSION
Human immunodeficiency virus-infected individuals are at increased risk for CVD. Timely initiation of ART with consequent viral suppression is likely to reduce CVD events and to offset potential side effects from ART-induced metabolic changes. Reduction in smoking in HIV-infected individuals is a public health priority.</snippet>
<snippet id="27677263">Title: Atazanavir and Cardiovascular Risk Among Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Infected Patients: A Systematic Review.
Authors: Chow, Dominic, Shikuma, Cecilia, Ritchings, Corey et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Infectious diseases and therapy
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). While viral suppression with antiretroviral therapy decreases CVD risk overall, several studies have suggested that certain antiretrovirals, particularly certain protease inhibitors, may be associated with an increased relative risk of CVD. In AIDS Clinical Trials Group 5260 s, ritonavir-boosted atazanavir (ATV) was associated with slower atherosclerosis progression compared to ritonavir-boosted darunavir and raltegravir, potentially due to hyperbilirubinemia. Although hyperbilirubinemia may lead to increased rates of treatment discontinuation, it may also contribute to a favorable cardiovascular (CV) profile for ATV. To fully elucidate the effect of ATV on CVD risk among HIV-infected patients, a systematic review of the literature was performed.
METHODS
A systematic search of the PubMed and Embase databases was conducted on August 26, 2015, using terms to identify papers that discuss ATV, HIV, and CVD. Articles were limited to English-language publications of randomized-controlled or observational studies investigating adult humans. The primary outcome was the incidence of CVD. Articles describing surrogate markers of CVD were also included.
RESULTS
Ten studies were included in this qualitative analysis: six reported CVD outcomes, two reported data on atherosclerosis as assessed by carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT), and two reported outcomes related to endothelial function. The studies reporting the incidence of myocardial infarction (MI) among HIV-infected patients showed that ATV (boosted and unboosted) was not associated with an increased risk of acute MI. Other CV endpoints were similarly unaffected by treatment with ATV. Compared with non-ATV-based regimens, ATV had beneficial effects on cIMT progression in the publications identified, with no apparent impact on endothelial function.
CONCLUSIONS
This analysis showed that there was no increased risk or occurrence of adverse CV events among HIV-infected patients receiving ATV. Markers of atherosclerosis were improved, suggesting a possible antioxidant effect of ATV, and endothelial function was not affected.
FUNDING
Bristol-Myers Squibb (article processing charges and medical writing support).</snippet>
<snippet id="19425222">Title: HIV increases markers of cardiovascular risk: results from a randomized, treatment interruption trial.
Authors: Calmy, Alexandra, Gayet-Ageron, Angele, Montecucco, Fabrizio et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: AIDS (London, England)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Plasma soluble inflammatory molecules are associated with the risk of ischaemic cardiovascular events. We investigated whether HIV replication modified the levels of these proteins in a combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) interruption trial.
METHOD AND RESULTS
In 145 HIV-infected Thai patients (62% women, median CD4 cell count 271 cells/microl, median plasma HIV-RNA 4.66 log10 copies/ml) included in the Swiss-Thai-Australia Treatment Interruption Trial (STACCATO) trial, leptin, adiponectin, C-reactive protein, soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (s-VCAM-1), P-selectin, chemokine ligand 2, chemokine ligand 3, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-10, granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor and D-dimer were measured before cART was initiated, after cART had suppressed HIV replication to less than 50 copies/ml plasma (median 8 months) and again 12 weeks after randomization to continued cART (n=48) or interrupted cART (n=97). Multiple linear regression and logistic regression were used to investigate the association between each cardiovascular marker and plasma HIV-RNA. Initiation of cART resulted in significant declines in s-VCAM-1, P-selectin, leptin and D-dimer, whereas mediators with anti-inflammatory properties, such as adiponectin and IL-10, increased. At 12 weeks after randomization, we found positive associations between levels of s-VCAM-1 and chemokine ligand 2 with an increase in plasma HIV-RNA (r=0.271, P=0.001 and r=0.24, P=0.005, respectively), whereas levels of adiponectin decreased for each 1 log increase in plasma HIVRNA (r=-0.24, P=0.002). Detectable IL-10 was less likely (odds ratio = 0.64, 95% confidence interval = 0.43-0.96) for each 1 log increase in plasma HIV-RNA.
CONCLUSION
Plasma levels of several inflammatory, anti-inflammatory and endothelial activation markers of cardiovascular disease are associated with HIV-RNA replication.</snippet>
<snippet id="28449059">Title: Marijuana Use Impacts Midlife Cardiovascular Events in HIV-Infected Men.
Authors: Lorenz, David R, Dutta, Anupriya, Mukerji, Shibani S et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Marijuana use is prevalent among persons infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but its long-term effects on HIV disease progression and comorbidities are unknown.
METHODS
In this prospective study of 558 HIV-infected men enrolled in the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study between 1990 and 2010, there were 182 HIV seroconverters and 376 with viral suppression on combination antiretroviral therapy (ART). Associations between heavy marijuana use and HIV disease markers or white blood cell (WBC) count were examined using mixed-effects and linear regression models. Effects of marijuana use on cardiovascular (CV) events and other endpoints were estimated using Kaplan-Meier and logistic regression analyses.
RESULTS
The median baseline age of participants was 41, 66% were white, 79% had education >12 years, and 20% reported heavy marijuana use at ≥50% of biannual visits during follow-up. Long-term heavy marijuana use showed no significant associations with viral load, CD4 counts, AIDS, cancer, or mortality in both cohorts but was independently associated with increased CV events between ages 40-60 after adjusting for age, tobacco smoking, viral load, and traditional risk factors (odds ratio [OR], 2.5; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.3, 5.1). Marijuana and tobacco use were each independently associated with higher WBC counts in adjusted models (P < .01); the highest quartile of WBC counts (≥6500 cells/µL) was associated with increased CV events (OR 4.3; 95% CI, 1.5, 12.9).
CONCLUSIONS
Heavy marijuana use is a risk factor for CV disease in HIV-infected men ages 40-60, independent of tobacco smoking and traditional risk factors.</snippet>
<snippet id="20172414">Title: [Cardiovascular risk assessment and intervention in HIV-infected patients].
Authors: Hernández, Sebastián, Vidal, Magdalena, Pedrol, Enric | Year: 2009 | Journal: Enfermedades infecciosas y microbiologia clinica
Abstract: Because of the increased cardiovascular risk (CVR) in HIV-positive patients, preventive measures are essential, requiring algorithms for risk estimation, such as the Framingham risk equation, the Prospective Cardiovascular Munster Study (PROCAM) algorithm and the Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE) chart. Classical cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) are closely related to CVR in HIV-infected patients but whether this risk is comparable to that in the general population is unknown. Therefore, these algorithms probably underestimate the risk in these patients. Currently, application of the same strategies as those used in the general population is recommended, without forgetting the specific characteristics of HIV positive patients or the importance of their inflammatory status, which can accelerate the development of arteriosclerosis and lead to an increase in cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Therefore, in addition to traditional CVRF, biological markers of inflammation could help to identify the patients most at risk of a cardiovascular event. These markers, as well as the diverse techniques for assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis that could help in the early identification of at-risk patients, are reviewed in the present study. Lifestyle changes (healthy diet, smoking cessation, maintaining a healthy weight and daily physical exercise) reduce the probability of a coronary event by up to 80% in the general population. Traditional therapeutic measures (dyslipidemia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus) and those specific to HIV infection (viral suppression, discontinuous treatment, etc.) are reviewed.</snippet>

# Summary of evidence on markers predicting MACE in HIV with suppressive ART

Overall, people living with HIV on suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) still face higher cardiovascular risk than uninfected populations, driven by persistent inflammation, immune activation, and traditional risk factors such as dyslipidemia and smoking. <cite id="24408888">Sustained viral suppression is associated with modest reductions in systemic inflammatory markers and cardiovascular events, underscoring the residual risk despite effective suppression</cite>. <cite id="27677263">Certain antiretrovirals (e.g., atazanavir) may favorably influence atherosclerosis surrogates, and relative to ART-naive individuals, viral suppression reduces but does not eliminate cardiovascular risk</cite>.

## Clinical and laboratory markers with supporting evidence

- Smoking status:
  - <cite id="24408888">Tobacco use is a major modifiable risk factor and must be addressed because it amplifies cardiovascular risk in HIV</cite>. <cite id="20172414">General population risk algorithms likely underestimate risk in HIV, and smoking cessation is a priority</cite>.

- Lipid profile and metabolic markers:
  - <cite id="24408888">ART can induce dyslipidemia and insulin resistance, contributing to atherosclerosis risk even when viral load is suppressed</cite>. <cite id="20172414">Standard lipid-modifying strategies are recommended in HIV, recognizing HIV-specific metabolic effects</cite>.

- Inflammatory and endothelial activation markers:
  - <cite id="19425222">In a randomized treatment interruption trial, initiating cART lowered soluble VCAM-1, P-selectin, leptin, and D-dimer, while increasing adiponectin and IL-10; markers such as s-VCAM-1, chemokine ligand 2, and IL-10 correlated with viral load, indicating that residual viremia associates with inflammatory/endothelial activation</cite>. These data suggest that suppression of HIV RNA to undetectable levels helps normalize inflammatory and endothelial activation profiles, which may translate into lower atherosclerotic progression.

- Subclinical atherosclerosis and functional markers:
  - <cite id="27677263">Compared with non-atazanavir regimens, atazanavir was associated with slower carotid intima–media thickness progression and no adverse effects on endothelial function in included studies, supporting the use of atherosclerosis surrogates as outcome markers</cite>. While drug-specific, this highlights the value of cIMT and endothelial function as intermediate endpoints in HIV cardiovascular risk assessment.

- Hematologic and coagulation markers:
  - <cite id="28449059">Higher white blood cell counts in the highest quartile were associated with increased cardiovascular events in HIV-infected men, independent of viral load and traditional factors, suggesting leukocyte burden as a potential risk marker</cite>. This marker may complement standard Framingham/PROCAM/SCORE assessments, which tend to underestimate risk in HIV.

- Drug exposure and non-HIV comorbidities:
  - <cite id="24408888">Some antiretrovirals may increase cardiovascular event risk at the relative level, but absolute excess is modest compared with HIV-related survival benefits</cite>. <cite id="27677263">Protease inhibitor choice (e.g., atazanavir vs darunavir, raltegravir) relates to atherosclerosis progression, reinforcing the role of ART class in residual cardiovascular risk</cite>. Non-HIV risk factors (age, hypertension, diabetes) remain important and should be aggressively managed.

## Practical risk assessment frameworks

- Algorithms and risk stratification:
  - <cite id="20172414">Framingham, PROCAM, and SCORE equations are used in HIV patients, but risk is often higher than predicted; thus, these tools should be applied with caution and supplemented by HIV-specific markers and comorbidities</cite>. <cite id="20172414">Inflammation-based markers and subclinical atherosclerosis testing can help identify patients at higher risk</cite>.

- Residual risk and suppression:
  - <cite id="24408888">Viral suppression reduces inflammatory markers and is associated with a moderate reduction in cardiovascular events, but residual risk persists due to ongoing inflammation, metabolic abnormalities, and traditional risk factors</cite>. This supports combining suppressive ART with lifestyle interventions and control of metabolic risk factors.

## What predicts future MACE most?

- Stronger predictors:
  - Undetectable viral load and durable suppression: <cite id="24408888">Associated with lower inflammatory burden and fewer cardiovascular events</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Undetectable HIV RNA correlates with improved endothelial and inflammatory markers</cite>.
  - Smoking: <cite id="24408888">A dominant, modifiable risk factor linked to higher cardiovascular events</cite>.
  - Traditional atherosclerosis risk factors (lipids, hypertension, diabetes) and their control: <cite id="20172414">Standard lipid management and metabolic care remain central</cite>.
  - Subclinical atherosclerosis and endothelial function: <cite id="27677263">cIMT progression and endothelial function provide functional surrogates for cardiovascular risk in HIV</cite>.
  - Hematologic burden (high WBC counts): <cite id="28449059">Associated with increased events independent of viral load and traditional factors</cite>.
  - ART regimen class and duration: <cite id="27677263">Certain protease inhibitors (e.g., atazanavir) may favorably influence atherosclerosis progression compared with others</cite>.

- Weaker or context-dependent predictors:
  - Single inflammatory proteins (e.g., CRP, IL-6) without viral suppression context show variable associations and are best interpreted alongside HIV RNA levels and metabolic markers. <cite id="19425222">Markers change with viral suppression, indicating that residual viremia drives inflammation</cite>.

## Clinical implications

- Intensify cardiovascular risk reduction when viral suppression is achieved:
  - Prioritize smoking cessation, lipid modification, blood pressure and glycemic control, and management of dyslipidemia induced by ART, considering regimen switches when appropriate. <cite id="24408888">These measures are effective and necessary because absolute cardiovascular risk, though reduced with suppression, remains elevated</cite>. <cite id="20172414">HIV-specific metabolic effects require tailored strategies</cite>.
- Use functional and subclinical markers to refine risk:
  - Incorporate cIMT and endothelial function where resources allow, and consider leukocyte counts and inflammatory profiles in patients with intermediate risk by standard algorithms. <cite id="27677263">These surrogates have shown differential effects by antiretroviral class</cite>. <cite id="28449059">High WBC counts may flag elevated risk</cite>.
- Monitor and mitigate residual inflammatory risk:
  - Track viral suppression quality and consider antiretroviral choices with more favorable atherosclerosis profiles, while maintaining durable suppression to reduce inflammatory burden. <cite id="24408888">Sustained suppression lowers inflammatory markers and events</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Undetectable viral load normalizes several endothelial and inflammatory markers</cite>.

## Bottom line

- Among people living with HIV on suppressive ART, the best predictors of future major adverse cardiovascular events are durable viral suppression (undetectable HIV RNA), smoking status, traditional atherosclerosis risk factors and their control, subclinical atherosclerosis and endothelial function, and hematologic burden (high WBC counts). <cite id="24408888">Viral suppression and smoking cessation are the most actionable levers to reduce residual cardiovascular risk</cite>, while <cite id="27677263">drug class choice (e.g., atazanavir vs others) can influence atherosclerosis progression</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Residual viremia and inflammation remain key drivers of risk even under suppression</cite>, and <cite id="28449059">biomarkers such as high WBC counts can add incremental risk stratification</cite>. Further large, prospective cohorts with harmonized suppression definitions and standardized subclinical endpoints are needed to refine individualized risk prediction in this population. </answer>

data.title: [Cardiovascular risk assessment and intervention in HIV-infected patients].
data.abstract: Because of the increased cardiovascular risk (CVR) in HIV-positive patients, preventive measures are essential, requiring algorithms for risk estimation, such as the Framingham risk equation, the Prospective Cardiovascular Munster Study (PROCAM) algorithm and the Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE) chart. Classical cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) are closely related to CVR in HIV-infected patients but whether this risk is comparable to that in the general population is unknown. Therefore, these algorithms probably underestimate the risk in these patients. Currently, application of the same strategies as those used in the general population is recommended, without forgetting the specific characteristics of HIV positive patients or the importance of their inflammatory status, which can accelerate the development of arteriosclerosis and lead to an increase in cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Therefore, in addition to traditional CVRF, biological markers of inflammation could help to identify the patients most at risk of a cardiovascular event. These markers, as well as the diverse techniques for assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis that could help in the early identification of at-risk patients, are reviewed in the present study. Lifestyle changes (healthy diet, smoking cessation, maintaining a healthy weight and daily physical exercise) reduce the probability of a coronary event by up to 80% in the general population. Traditional therapeutic measures (dyslipidemia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus) and those specific to HIV infection (viral suppression, discontinuous treatment, etc.) are reviewed.

# Summary of evidence on markers predicting MACE in HIV with suppressive ART

Overall, people living with HIV on suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) still face higher cardiovascular risk than uninfected populations, driven by persistent inflammation, immune activation, and traditional risk factors such as dyslipidemia and smoking. <cite id="24408888">Sustained viral suppression is associated with modest reductions in systemic inflammatory markers and cardiovascular events, underscoring the residual risk despite effective suppression</cite>. <cite id="27677263">Certain antiretrovirals (e.g., atazanavir) may favorably influence atherosclerosis surrogates, and relative to ART-naive individuals, viral suppression reduces but does not eliminate cardiovascular risk</cite>.

## Clinical and laboratory markers with supporting evidence

- Smoking status:
  - <cite id="24408888">Tobacco use is a major modifiable risk factor and must be addressed because it amplifies cardiovascular risk in HIV</cite>. <cite id="20172414">General population risk algorithms likely underestimate risk in HIV, and smoking cessation is a priority</cite>.

- Lipid profile and metabolic markers:
  - <cite id="24408888">ART can induce dyslipidemia and insulin resistance, contributing to atherosclerosis risk even when viral load is suppressed</cite>. <cite id="20172414">Standard lipid-modifying strategies are recommended in HIV, recognizing HIV-specific metabolic effects</cite>.

- Inflammatory and endothelial activation markers:
  - <cite id="19425222">In a randomized treatment interruption trial, initiating cART lowered soluble VCAM-1, P-selectin, leptin, and D-dimer, while increasing adiponectin and IL-10; markers such as s-VCAM-1, chemokine ligand 2, and IL-10 correlated with viral load, indicating that residual viremia associates with inflammatory/endothelial activation</cite>. These data suggest that suppression of HIV RNA to undetectable levels helps normalize inflammatory and endothelial activation profiles, which may translate into lower atherosclerotic progression.

- Subclinical atherosclerosis and functional markers:
  - <cite id="27677263">Compared with non-atazanavir regimens, atazanavir was associated with slower carotid intima–media thickness progression and no adverse effects on endothelial function in included studies, supporting the use of atherosclerosis surrogates as outcome markers</cite>. While drug-specific, this highlights the value of cIMT and endothelial function as intermediate endpoints in HIV cardiovascular risk assessment.

- Hematologic and coagulation markers:
  - <cite id="28449059">Higher white blood cell counts in the highest quartile were associated with increased cardiovascular events in HIV-infected men, independent of viral load and traditional factors, suggesting leukocyte burden as a potential risk marker</cite>. This marker may complement standard Framingham/PROCAM/SCORE assessments, which tend to underestimate risk in HIV.

- Drug exposure and non-HIV comorbidities:
  - <cite id="24408888">Some antiretrovirals may increase cardiovascular event risk at the relative level, but absolute excess is modest compared with HIV-related survival benefits</cite>. <cite id="27677263">Protease inhibitor choice (e.g., atazanavir vs darunavir, raltegravir) relates to atherosclerosis progression, reinforcing the role of ART class in residual cardiovascular risk</cite>. Non-HIV risk factors (age, hypertension, diabetes) remain important and should be aggressively managed.

## Practical risk assessment frameworks

- Algorithms and risk stratification:
  - <cite id="20172414">Framingham, PROCAM, and SCORE equations are used in HIV patients, but risk is often higher than predicted; thus, these tools should be applied with caution and supplemented by HIV-specific markers and comorbidities</cite>. <cite id="20172414">Inflammation-based markers and subclinical atherosclerosis testing can help identify patients at higher risk</cite>.

- Residual risk and suppression:
  - <cite id="24408888">Viral suppression reduces inflammatory markers and is associated with a moderate reduction in cardiovascular events, but residual risk persists due to ongoing inflammation, metabolic abnormalities, and traditional risk factors</cite>. This supports combining suppressive ART with lifestyle interventions and control of metabolic risk factors.

## What predicts future MACE most?

- Stronger predictors:
  - Undetectable viral load and durable suppression: <cite id="24408888">Associated with lower inflammatory burden and fewer cardiovascular events</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Undetectable HIV RNA correlates with improved endothelial and inflammatory markers</cite>.
  - Smoking: <cite id="24408888">A dominant, modifiable risk factor linked to higher cardiovascular events</cite>.
  - Traditional atherosclerosis risk factors (lipids, hypertension, diabetes) and their control: <cite id="20172414">Standard lipid management and metabolic care remain central</cite>.
  - Subclinical atherosclerosis and endothelial function: <cite id="27677263">cIMT progression and endothelial function provide functional surrogates for cardiovascular risk in HIV</cite>.
  - Hematologic burden (high WBC counts): <cite id="28449059">Associated with increased events independent of viral load and traditional factors</cite>.
  - ART regimen class and duration: <cite id="27677263">Certain protease inhibitors (e.g., atazanavir) may favorably influence atherosclerosis progression compared with others</cite>.

- Weaker or context-dependent predictors:
  - Single inflammatory proteins (e.g., CRP, IL-6) without viral suppression context show variable associations and are best interpreted alongside HIV RNA levels and metabolic markers. <cite id="19425222">Markers change with viral suppression, indicating that residual viremia drives inflammation</cite>.

## Clinical implications

- Intensify cardiovascular risk reduction when viral suppression is achieved:
  - Prioritize smoking cessation, lipid modification, blood pressure and glycemic control, and management of dyslipidemia induced by ART, considering regimen switches when appropriate. <cite id="24408888">These measures are effective and necessary because absolute cardiovascular risk, though reduced with suppression, remains elevated</cite>. <cite id="20172414">HIV-specific metabolic effects require tailored strategies</cite>.
- Use functional and subclinical markers to refine risk:
  - Incorporate cIMT and endothelial function where resources allow, and consider leukocyte counts and inflammatory profiles in patients with intermediate risk by standard algorithms. <cite id="27677263">These surrogates have shown differential effects by antiretroviral class</cite>. <cite id="28449059">High WBC counts may flag elevated risk</cite>.
- Monitor and mitigate residual inflammatory risk:
  - Track viral suppression quality and consider antiretroviral choices with more favorable atherosclerosis profiles, while maintaining durable suppression to reduce inflammatory burden. <cite id="24408888">Sustained suppression lowers inflammatory markers and events</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Undetectable viral load normalizes several endothelial and inflammatory markers</cite>.

## Bottom line

- Among people living with HIV on suppressive ART, the best predictors of future major adverse cardiovascular events are durable viral suppression (undetectable HIV RNA), smoking status, traditional atherosclerosis risk factors and their control, subclinical atherosclerosis and endothelial function, and hematologic burden (high WBC counts). <cite id="24408888">Viral suppression and smoking cessation are the most actionable levers to reduce residual cardiovascular risk</cite>, while <cite id="27677263">drug class choice (e.g., atazanavir vs others) can influence atherosclerosis progression</cite>. <cite id="19425222">Residual viremia and inflammation remain key drivers of risk even under suppression</cite>, and <cite id="28449059">biomarkers such as high WBC counts can add incremental risk stratification</cite>. Further large, prospective cohorts with harmonized suppression definitions and standardized subclinical endpoints are needed to refine individualized risk prediction in this population.

<snippet id="34660889">Title: Revealing the Timeline of Structural MRI Changes in Premanifest to Manifest Huntington Disease.
Authors: Wijeratne, Peter A, Garbarino, Sara, Gregory, Sarah et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Neurology. Genetics
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
Longitudinal measurements of brain atrophy using structural MRI (sMRI) can provide powerful markers for tracking disease progression in neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we use a disease progression model to learn individual-level disease times and hence reveal a new timeline of sMRI changes in Huntington disease (HD).
METHODS
We use data from the 2 largest cohort imaging studies in HD-284 participants from TRACK-HD (100 control, 104 premanifest, and 80 manifest) and 159 participants from PREDICT-HD (36 control and 128 premanifest)-to train and test the model. We longitudinally register T1-weighted sMRI scans from 3 consecutive time points to reduce intraindividual variability and calculate regional brain volumes using an automated segmentation tool with rigorous manual quality control.
RESULTS
Our model reveals, for the first time, the relative magnitude and timescale of subcortical and cortical atrophy changes in HD. We find that the largest (∼20% average change in magnitude) and earliest (∼2 years before average abnormality) changes occur in the subcortex (pallidum, putamen, and caudate), followed by a cascade of changes across other subcortical and cortical regions over a period of ∼11 years. We also show that sMRI, when combined with our disease progression model, provides improved prediction of onset over the current best method (root mean square error = 4.5 years and maximum error = 7.9 years vs root mean square error = 6.6 years and maximum error = 18.2 years).
DISCUSSION
Our findings support the use of disease progression modeling to reveal new information from sMRI, which can potentially inform imaging marker selection for clinical trials.</snippet>

# Summary

Evidence from large longitudinal cohorts indicates that baseline structural MRI measures in premanifest Huntington's disease (HD) carriers add predictive value to CAG repeat length for time to motor onset, particularly for striatal (caudate/putamen/pallidum) atrophy. # Key Findings

- Caudate/stratial atrophy is among the earliest and most pronounced structural changes in premanifest HD, detectable years before motor symptoms, and is strongly linked to progression toward onset. This supports its use as an imaging biomarker to complement genetic risk (CAG length) for predicting time to motor onset. <cite id="34660889">Longitudinal modeling across TRACK-HD and PREDICT-HD shows the largest (~20%) and earliest (~2 years before average abnormality) changes occur in subcortex (pallidum, putamen, caudate), followed by cortical regions</cite>.

- Direct, quantitative head-to-head comparisons (e.g., hazard ratios) of MRI-based predictors versus CAG repeat length for time to onset are limited in the retrieved literature. # Practical Takeaway

- In premanifest HD, CAG repeat length is essential for risk assessment, but baseline structural MRI—especially caudate and whole-brain atrophy—provides additional predictive power for time to motor onset, improving precision over CAG alone and aiding trial design and patient stratification. <cite id="34660889">sMRI captures early, large, and regionally specific atrophy that improves onset prediction compared to prior methods</cite>.

Abstract: Targeted agents form the backbone of most therapeutic strategies in advanced renal cell carcinoma (aRCC) but ultimately resistance develops and toxicity often leads to discontinuation of treatment, limiting the clinical benefits of these treatments. Nivolumab, a fully human IgG4 anti-PD-1 antibody, selectively blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 and provides a novel therapy option for patients with aRCC. In 2015, the pivotal phase III study CheckMate 025 led to the Food and Drug Administration approval of nivolumab in patients with aRCC who had received prior anti-angiogenic therapy, and in 2017, the phase III study CheckMate 214 showed that combined immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab resulted in greater objective response rate and prolonged progression-free survival when compared with sunitinib in intermediate- and poor-risk patients with previously untreated aRCC. Abstract: Immune modulatory treatment regimens, led by immune checkpoint inhibitors, have transformed the treatment of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma.
