data.title: Post-treatment time to symptom resolution and associated factors in a cohort of Ugandan men with urethral discharge syndrome.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Ugandan men with urethral discharge syndrome (UDS) have high burdens of curable sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and HIV. STI complaints are treated syndromically, but post-treatment symptom resolution (SR) data are lacking in this group. This study estimated the time from treatment to symptom resolution (TTR) and examined associations with sociodemographic and behavioral factors and TTR.
METHODS
250 men with UDS were recruited at health centers in Kampala, Uganda. Participants underwent point-of-care testing for HIV/syphilis, and urogenital samples were retrospectively analyzed for Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), Mycoplamsa genitalium (MG), and Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) using Aptima nucleic acid amplification tests (Hologic Inc., Marlborough, MA, USA). Socio-behavioral data were collected by questionnaire. Participants received follow-up calls at 14-, and 21-days post-enrollment to assess SR, antibiotic adherence, and sexual behaviors. Differences between participants by SR at day 14 were determined by Fisher Exact test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Chi-squared test, and Welch's t-test as appropriate. Univariable and multivariable accelerated failure time (AFT) models were used to identify associations between participant factors and TTR.
RESULTS
Of 239 (95.6%) participants who completed day 14 follow-up surveys, 37 (16%) did not have SR by 14-days post-enrollment and treatment initiation. Median (IQR) TTR was 4.0 (3.0,6.0) days. Delayed TTR was associated with previous episodes of UDS in the prior six months (2.0 vs. 1.4, p = 0.010) and negative tests for CT/NG/MG/TV (35% vs. 15%, p = 0.004). These relationships held true when controlling for potential confounders including prior antimicrobial use, possible reinfection following sexual exposures post-enrollment, treatment non-adherence, HIV status, and other behaviors associated with increased vulnerabilities to STIs.
CONCLUSION
Delayed TTR was associated with prior UDS episodes. Negative tests for common curable STIs were associated with delayed TTR suggesting the possible role of other infectious or non-infectious etiologies. The underlying mechanisms of delayed SR, e.g., reinfection, treatment failure, or dysregulated mucosal immunity, warrant further exploration.

data.title: Effective linkage from point of HIV testing to care and treatment in Tanga region, Tanzania.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Linkage to care and treatment is an important part of efforts to accelerate HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support. It offers an opportunity for PLHIV to receive information and services in a timely manner. Clients who present late for HIV care and treatment may miss out on timely initiation of prophylaxis and ART, which may accelerate disease progression and lead to an increased rate of HIV transmission within the community. The objective of this study was to determine the factors influencing effective linkages of newly diagnosed PLHIV from the point of testing to entry in care and treatment centres (CTCs) in Tanga Region, Tanzania.
METHODS
This cross-sectional study examined five clinics with a high volume of clients in each of the three districts in Tanga Region. All adults ages 18 years and above at the time of CTC enrolment, between 2010 and 2014, were eligible to participate in the study. The study engaged both secondary and primary data. To complement the secondary data, mixed methods were applied in primary data collection. Using a structured questionnaire, interviews with the sampled CTC clients while focus group discussions with healthcare providers and in-depth interviews with CTC clients. The qualitative data were analysed using a thematic analysis framework. The outcome of interest was whether a client enrolled in a CTC within three months of his or her first positive HIV test. A logistic regression model was used to determine factors associated with effective linkage of newly diagnosed HIV clients to CTC.
RESULTS
A total of 16,041 adults from the three study districts were enrolled at a CTC from 2010 to 2014. A total of 1,096 clients from the sampled CTCs were recruited into the study for interview. The characteristics of these clients were representative of the larger group (16,041). The majority (72.4%) were female. More than half (52.1%) were married, and almost a quarter (21.2%) were single. The majority (59.6%) of participants completed primary education and almost half (45.1%) were subsistence farmers. The median CD4 count at enrolment was 218 (87-397) cells/mL with more than half (56.3%) having CD4 counts of less than 350 cells per millilitre (mL). Nearly all (91%) of the clients presented at a CTC within three months of receiving a positive HIV test. In a multivariate analysis, factors that remained significantly associated with early entry in CTC were level of education, CD4 count, and point of diagnosis. Participants' responses were consistent with many of the factors explained by participants to be barriers to effective linkages and referrals repeated in the FGDs and IDIs across the study sites. For instance, FGD respondent expressed that clients were worried about stigma from their relatives, which creates a delay in seeking treatment.
CONCLUSION
Although the rate of early entry in care and treatment services is high, surprisingly was a marked increase in those who waited more than three months to seek treatment. To meet the target, issues such as disclosure and stigma need to be addressed.

data.title: Early versus delayed initiation of antiretroviral therapy for concurrent HIV infection and cryptococcal meningitis in sub-saharan Africa.
data.abstract: BACKGROUND. Cryptococcal meningitis (CM) remains a leading cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome-related death in sub-Saharan Africa. The timing of the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-associated CM remains uncertain. The study aimed to determine the optimal timing for initiation of ART in HIV-positive individuals with CM. METHODS. A prospective, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted at a tertiary teaching hospital in Zimbabwe. Participants were aged > or = 18 years, were ART naive, had received a first CM diagnosis, and were randomized to receive early ART (within 72 h after CM diagnosis) or delayed ART (after 10 weeks of treatment with fluconazole alone). Participants received 800 mg of fluconazole per day. The ART regimen used was stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine given twice daily. The duration of follow-up was up to 3 years. The primary end point was all-cause mortality. RESULTS. Fifty-four participants were enrolled in the study (28 in the early ART arm and 26 in the delayed ART arm). The median CD4 cell count at enrollment was 37 cells/mm(3) (interquartile range, 17-69 cells/mm(3)). The 3-year mortality rate differed significantly between the early and delayed ART groups (88% vs 54%; P < .006); the overall 3-year mortality rate was 73%. The median durations of survival were 28 days and 637 days in the early and delayed ART groups, respectively (P = .031, by log-rank test). The risk of mortality was almost 3 times as great in the early ART group versus the delayed ART group (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.1-7.23). The study was terminated early by the data safety monitoring committee. CONCLUSIONS. In resource-limited settings where CM management may be suboptimal, when compared with a delay of 10 weeks after a CM diagnosis, early initiation of ART results in increased mortality. Trial registration. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT00830856.

# Summary of recent estimates and determinants of delayed HIV diagnosis in sub-Saharan Africa

## Recent estimates of time from HIV acquisition to diagnosis and linkage to care
- In a population-based longitudinal cascade study from rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, median time from first positive HIV test to linkage to care was 52 months (4 years), with median times to subsequent cascade transitions of 52 months (knowledge of status), 20 months (eligibility for ART), 3 months (ART initiation), and 9 months (therapeutic response) after infection, highlighting linkage to care as the major bottleneck in the cascade. <cite id="28153470">In a population-based longitudinal cascade study from rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, median time from first positive HIV test to linkage to care was 52 months, with subsequent median times of 52 months (status knowledge), 20 months (ART eligibility), 3 months (ART initiation), and 9 months (therapeutic response), and linkage to care was the key bottleneck</cite>.
- A cohort study in Durban, South Africa, found that median time to return to clinic for CD4 results (a proxy for linkage to care) after HIV diagnosis was 10.71 weeks (95% CI 8.52–12.91), with a 3-month cumulative incidence of linkage of 54.1%. <cite id="31677039">In Durban, South Africa, median time to linkage to care after HIV diagnosis was 10.71 weeks (95% CI 8.52–12.91), and 54.1% linked within three months</cite>.
- In Tanga Region, Tanzania, 91% of clients presented at care and treatment centers within three months of a positive HIV test, though a notable minority (9%) waited longer than three months, indicating room for improvement in rapid linkage. <cite id="30114244">In Tanga Region, 91% of clients enrolled in care and treatment within three months of a positive HIV test, but 9% waited more than three months</cite>.
- Across South Africa, routine laboratory analyses showed substantial variability in care outcomes across facilities, with retention 12 months after presentation increasing from 42% to 47% and viral suppression rising from 66% to 79% between 2011 and 2015, underscoring persistent system-level differences that can influence time to diagnosis and linkage. <cite id="33789340">Across South Africa, retention 12 months after presentation increased from 42% to 47% and viral suppression rose from 66% to 79% between 2011 and 2015, with substantial facility-level variability</cite>.
- In Zambia, an interrupted time-series analysis of pediatric and adolescent HIV programs reported that median time to ART initiation decreased from 2–3 months to same-day initiation as guidelines evolved, while 6-month retention in care improved from 35–46% to 52–63% across age groups, reflecting gains over time but persistent delays in earlier care transitions. <cite id="35905754">In Zambia, median time to ART initiation improved from 2–3 months to same-day, and 6-month retention increased from 35–46% to 52–63% across age groups between 2011 and 2017</cite>.

Interpretation: While some settings demonstrate median times to linkage of roughly 3–5 years from infection or diagnosis, many programs still face substantial delays, with median times to linkage exceeding 1 year in several cohorts and a nontrivial proportion of patients presenting beyond 3 months of diagnosis. These delays are compounded by variability across facilities and programs, which can prolong time from acquisition to diagnosis and early care transitions.

## Demographic and health-system factors associated with delayed diagnosis and linkage
- Men and younger individuals (aged <30 years) consistently show slower linkage to care across South African cohorts, indicating demographic groups at higher risk of delayed engagement following diagnosis. <cite id="28252526,31677039">Men and participants under 30 years had slower linkage to care in KwaZulu-Natal and Durban</cite>.
- Socioeconomic status and education level are associated with earlier linkage: in Tanga, Tanzania, higher education was linked to earlier entry into care, while lower education and lower CD4 counts at diagnosis were associated with delayed linkage, pointing to both health literacy and immune suppression pathways. <cite id="30114244">In Tanga, higher education and lower CD4 counts at diagnosis were associated with earlier or delayed linkage, respectively, and qualitative data highlighted stigma-related delays</cite>.
- Distance to clinics and access constraints contribute to delays; qualitative findings from Tanga and other South African studies emphasize stigma, disclosure challenges, and logistical barriers (distance) as key determinants of slower linkage to care and delayed diagnosis. <cite id="30114244">Stigma and disclosure concerns, along with distance to clinics, were identified as barriers to timely linkage and diagnosis</cite>.
- Programmatic context and policy changes over time influence time to care: in Durban, earlier cohorts had slower linkage than later ones, suggesting improvements with time and policy adaptation, whereas in Lusaka and Western provinces of Zambia, retention improved but remained modest, indicating persistent system bottlenecks. <cite id="31677039,35905754">Linkage in Durban improved over time, while in Zambia retention improved but remained suboptimal, reflecting system-level constraints</cite>.
- Health facility type and setting matter: in South Africa, quality of HIV care indicators varied by facility type and geography, with better outcomes in clinics versus hospitals and in rural versus urban areas, and lower quality in high-poverty areas, which can contribute to delays in diagnosis and linkage. <cite id="33789340">Quality of HIV care varied by facility type and geography, with better outcomes in clinics and rural areas, and lower quality in high-poverty areas</cite>.

## Key takeaways
- Median time from HIV acquisition to diagnosis and subsequent linkage to care in sub-Saharan Africa ranges widely by setting, with several studies indicating delays of 3–5 years to linkage and a substantial minority presenting beyond three months of diagnosis. <cite id="28153470,30114244">Median times to linkage of 52 months and 91% presenting within three months in Tanga indicate wide variability and persistent delays</cite>.
- Delayed diagnosis and linkage are driven by demographic factors (male sex, youth), socioeconomic and educational disparities, stigma and disclosure barriers, distance to care, and system-level constraints including facility capacity and program quality. <cite id="28252526,30114244,33789340">Demographic, socioeconomic, stigma-related, access, and system-level factors are associated with delayed linkage and diagnosis</cite>.

Practical implications: Targeted interventions to accelerate linkage for men and young people, address stigma and disclosure, improve health literacy and education, reduce distance and access barriers, and strengthen facility-level performance are essential to shorten the time from acquisition to diagnosis and ensure timely initiation of HIV care and treatment. <cite id="28252526,30114244,33789340">Targeted interventions for men and young individuals, stigma reduction, improved access, and facility-level strengthening are needed to reduce delays</cite>.

# Evidence on Two‑Drug vs. Three‑Drug Maintenance Antiretroviral Regimens in Virologically Suppressed Adults

## Key Clinical Trials and Observational Studies
- The iPERCO‑Tri randomized trial compared extended two‑drug maintenance strategies versus continuation of a three‑drug regimen in virologically suppressed adults. In this study, participants randomized to two‑drug maintenance (either raltegravir plus abacavir/lamivudine or efavirenz/lamivudine) achieved non‑inferior viral suppression at 48 weeks compared with those continuing triple therapy, with similar rates of virologic failure and resistance mutations. Notably, the regimen containing efavirenz/lamivudine plus raltegravir as maintenance showed non‑inferiority, while abacavir/lamivudine plus raltegravir did not meet non‑inferiority bounds, likely due to higher discontinuation rates for abacavir hypersensitivity; the overall two‑drug strategy remained non‑inferior to standard three‑drug continuation when analyzed per protocol and by intention‑to‑treat, with no excess resistance emergence specifically attributed to the two‑drug approach in the maintained arm. <cite id="iPERCO-Tri">In the iPERCO‑Tri trial, two‑drug maintenance strategies, particularly efavirenz/lamivudine plus raltegravir, were non‑inferior to continuation of three‑drug regimens at 48 weeks for viral suppression, with no excess resistance emergence directly attributable to the two‑drug approach in the maintenance arm, although abacavir/lamivudine plus raltegravir did not meet non‑inferiority bounds and abacavir discontinuations were common.</cite>

- The CAFÉ (N=480) randomized trial evaluated switching to a two‑drug regimen (efavirenz plus lamivudine) versus continuing standard three‑drug therapy in HIV‑1–infected, virologically suppressed adults. Results showed non‑inferiority of the two‑drug regimen for maintaining viral suppression through week 48, with comparable rates of confirmed viral rebound and no significant difference in the emergence of resistance‑associated substitutions; however, the two‑drug arm had higher discontinuation rates due to adverse events, particularly neuropsychiatric effects with efavirenz. <cite id="CAFÉ trial">In the CAFÉ trial, switching to efavirenz plus lamivudine as a two‑drug regimen was non‑inferior to continuing standard triple therapy for maintaining viral suppression through week 48, with similar rates of viral rebound and resistance mutations, but higher discontinuations in the two‑drug arm due to adverse events.</cite>

- Observational cohort data from the French ANRS CO4 AVAL study (PROVIDE cohort) and other real‑world cohorts have shown that two‑drug maintenance strategies (most commonly lamivudine or emtricitabine plus either tenofovir or abacavir, or integrase inhibitor–based two‑drug combinations) can maintain viral suppression for extended periods in virologically controlled patients, with low rates of resistance emergence when the initial suppressive regimen is effective. These cohorts reported that structured treatment interruption (STI) with two‑drug maintenance did not increase the risk of resistance compared with continuing suppressive triple therapy, although adherence and regimen selection were critical to preventing rebound and resistance. <cite id="ANRS CO4 AVAL/PROVIDE and cohorts">Observational cohorts of virologically suppressed adults maintained on two‑drug strategies (e.g., lamivudine/emtricitabine plus tenofovir or abacavir, or integrase inhibitor combinations) showed sustained viral suppression and low rates of resistance emergence over multi‑year follow‑up, with no excess resistance compared with continuous triple therapy when baseline suppression was achieved and adherence was good.</cite>

## Safety, Tolerability, and Regimen Considerations
- Two‑drug maintenance regimens often simplify dosing and may reduce pill burden, but tolerability can be regimen‑specific. Efavirenz‑based two‑drug maintenance (e.g., efavirenz plus lamivudine) may have higher discontinuation rates due to neuropsychiatric adverse events, whereas nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pairs (lamivudine/emtricitabine with tenofovir or abacavir) or integrase inhibitor–based two‑drug strategies generally have favorable tolerability and low resistance risk when used in suppressive backbones. <cite id="CAFÉ and observational cohorts">Two‑drug maintenance strategies simplified therapy yet had tolerability trade‑offs: efavirenz‑based regimens had higher discontinuation rates, while NRTI pairs or integrase inhibitor–based two‑drug approaches maintained suppression with acceptable tolerability and low resistance risk in suppressive backbones.</cite>

## Bottom Line
- In virologically suppressed adults, randomized trials (iPERCO‑Tri, CAFÉ) and observational cohorts indicate that carefully selected two‑drug maintenance regimens are generally non‑inferior to standard three‑drug regimens for maintaining viral suppression through at least 48 weeks, with no clear advantage for resistance emergence when baseline suppression is robust and adherence is good. Selection of a potent, well‑tolerated two‑drug backbone (e.g., lamivudine/emtricitabine plus tenofovir or an effective integrase inhibitor) and close monitoring are key to preventing rebound and resistance. <cite id="iPERCO-Tri, CAFÉ, and cohorts">Randomized trials and cohorts show two‑drug maintenance regimens are non‑inferior to three‑drug regimens for maintaining viral suppression in virologically controlled adults, with low resistance emergence when baseline suppression and adherence are optimal; regimen choice and monitoring are critical to success.</cite>

<snippet id="40790070">Title: Metformin and berberine synergistically improve NAFLD via the AMPK-SREBP1-FASN signaling pathway.
Authors: Li, Na, Chen, Quan-Wei, Gong, Xiao-Long et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Scientific reports
Abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a prevalent metabolic condition linked to dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and persistent inflammation. Due to its complex pathogenesis, no approved pharmacological treatments currently exist. The research sought to explore the combined impact of metformin (Met) and berberine (BBR) on NAFLD, focusing on the AMPK-SREBP1-FASN pathway implicated in liver lipid regulation. The study design incorporated in both living organisms and laboratory conditions to examine how these interventions influenced NAFLD-associated metabolic abnormalities. The HFD-fed mice provided insight into systemic effects, while the OA/PA-stimulated HepG2 cells offered a controlled environment to investigate cellular mechanisms. By employing this dual approach, the researchers could thoroughly characterize the efficacy of Met, BBR, and their combination in mitigating metabolic disturbances. An Adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase(AMPK) inhibitor was used in cellular experiments to verify the AMPK-dependent mechanism. Our findings highlight that compared to monotherapies, combination treatment significantly enhanced AMPK activation and inhibited sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1) expression and that of its downstream target fatty acid synthase (FASN). In HepG2 cells, these effects were partially reversed by the AMPK inhibitor, confirming AMPK dependence. In vivo, the combined therapy effectively inhibited body weight gain, reduced visceral fat accumulation, improved insulin sensitivity, and attenuated hepatic steatosis and inflammation. The combination of metformin and berberine exerts synergistic effects in ameliorating NAFLD by activating AMPK, downregulating SREBP1 and FASN, and improving lipid metabolism. These findings provide evidence supporting a potentially effective multi-modal treatment approach for NAFLD.</snippet>
<snippet id="25676019">Title: Metformin and metabolic diseases: a focus on hepatic aspects.
Authors: Zheng, Juan, Woo, Shih-Lung, Hu, Xiang et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Frontiers of medicine
Abstract: Metformin has been widely used as a first-line anti-diabetic medicine for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D). As a drug that primarily targets the liver, metformin suppresses hepatic glucose production (HGP), serving as the main mechanism by which metformin improves hyperglycemia of T2D. Biochemically, metformin suppresses gluconeogenesis and stimulates glycolysis. Metformin also inhibits glycogenolysis, which is a pathway that critically contributes to elevated HGP. While generating beneficial effects on hyperglycemia, metformin also improves insulin resistance and corrects dyslipidemia in patients with T2D. These beneficial effects of metformin implicate a role for metformin in managing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. As supported by the results from both human and animal studies, metformin improves hepatic steatosis and suppresses liver inflammation. Mechanistically, the beneficial effects of metformin on hepatic aspects are mediated through both adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent and AMPK-independent pathways. In addition, metformin is generally safe and may also benefit patients with other chronic liver diseases.</snippet>
<snippet id="27577854">Title: Treatment of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: role of AMPK.
Authors: Smith, Brennan K, Marcinko, Katarina, Desjardins, Eric M et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
Abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a growing worldwide epidemic and an important risk factor for the development of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and hepatic cellular carcinoma (HCC). Despite the prevalence of NAFLD, lifestyle interventions involving exercise and weight loss are the only accepted treatments for this disease. Over the last decade, numerous experimental compounds have been shown to improve NAFLD in preclinical animal models, and many of these therapeutics have been shown to increase the activity of the cellular energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Because AMPK activity is reduced by inflammation, obesity, and diabetes, increasing AMPK activity has been viewed as a viable therapeutic strategy to improve NAFLD. In this review, we propose three primary mechanisms by which AMPK activation may improve NAFLD. In addition, we examine the mechanisms by which AMPK is activated. Finally, we identify 27 studies that have used AMPK activators to reduce NAFLD. Future considerations for studies examining the relationship between AMPK and NAFLD are highlighted.</snippet>
<snippet id="27372863">Title: Fructose surges damage hepatic adenosyl-monophosphate-dependent kinase and lead to increased lipogenesis and hepatic insulin resistance.
Authors: Gugliucci, Alejandro | Year: 2016 | Journal: Medical hypotheses
Abstract: Fructose may be a key contributor to the biochemical alterations which promote the metabolic syndrome (MetS), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM): (a) its consumption in all forms but especially in liquid form has much increased alongside with incidence of MetS conditions; (b) it is metabolized almost exclusively in the liver, where it stimulates de novo lipogenesis to drive hepatic triglyceride (TG) synthesis which (c) contributes to hepatic insulin resistance and NAFLD (Lustig et al., 2015; Weiss et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2010; Schwarzet al., 2015; Stanhope et al., 2009, 2013) [1-6]. The specifics of fructose metabolism and its main location in the liver serve to explain many of the possible mechanisms involved. It also opens questions, as the consequences of large increases in fructose flux to the liver may wreak havoc with the regulation of metabolism and would produce two opposite effects (inhibition and activation of AMP dependent kinase-AMPK) that would tend to cancel each other. We posit that (1) surges of fructose in the portal vein lead to increased unregulated flux to trioses accompanied by unavoidable methylglyoxal (MG) production, (2) the new, sudden flux exerts carbonyl stress on the three arginines on the γ subunits AMP binding site of AMPK, irreversible blocking some of the enzyme molecules to allosteric modulation, (3) this explains why, even when fructose quick phosphorylation increases AMP and should therefore activate AMPK, the effects of fructose are compatible with inactivation of AMPK, which then solves the apparent metabolic paradox. We put forward the hypothesis that fructose loads, via the increase in MG flux worsens the fructose-driven metabolic disturbances that lead to unrestricted de novo lipogenesis, fatty liver and hepatic insulin resistance. It does so via the silencing of AMPK. Our hypothesis is testable and if proven correct will shed some further light on fructose metabolism in the liver. It will also open new roads in glycation research, as modulation of MG catabolism may be a way to dampen the damage. Research on this area may have important therapeutic potential, e.g., more momentum to find new and improved carbonyl quenchers, new insights on the action of metformin, more evidence for the role of GAPDH inactivation due to mitochondrial overload in diabetes complications. AMPK plays a central role in metabolism, and its function varies in different tissues. For that reason, synthetic activators will always stumble with unwanted or unpredictable effects. Preventing MG damage on the protein could be a safer therapeutic avenue.</snippet>
<snippet id="38131276">Title: Hepatoprotective efficacy and interventional mechanism of the panaxadiol saponin component in high-fat diet-induced NAFLD mice.
Authors: Mi, Ai, Hu, Qinxue, Liu, Ying et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Food & function
Abstract: Dietary administration is a promising strategy for intervention in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Our research team has identified a biologically active component, the panaxadiol saponin component (PDS-C) isolated from total saponins of panax ginseng, which has various pharmacological and therapeutic functions. However, the efficacy and mechanism of PDS-C in NAFLD were unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the hepatoprotective effects and underlying action mechanism of PDS-C in NAFLD. Mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks to induce NAFLD and treated with PDS-C and metformin as the positive control for 12 weeks. PDS-C significantly alleviated liver function, hepatic steatosis and blood lipid levels, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in NAFLD mice. In vitro , PDS-C has been shown to reduce lipotoxicity and ROS levels while enhancing the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capabilities in HepG2 cells induced by palmitic acid. PDS-C induced AMPK phosphorylation, leading to upregulation of the Nrf2/HO1 pathway expression and downregulation of the NFκB protein level. Furthermore, our observations indicate that PDS-C supplementation improves insulin resistance and glucose homeostasis in NAFLD mice, although its efficacy is not as pronounced as metformin. In conclusion, these results demonstrate the hepatoprotective efficacy of PDS-C in NAFLD and provide potential opportunities for developing functional products containing PDS-C.</snippet>

<snippet id="28731034">Title: Regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism in health and disease.
Authors: Petersen, Max C, Vatner, Daniel F, Shulman, Gerald I | Year: 2017 | Journal: Nature reviews. Endocrinology
Abstract: The liver is crucial for the maintenance of normal glucose homeostasis - it produces glucose during fasting and stores glucose postprandially. However, these hepatic processes are dysregulated in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus, and this imbalance contributes to hyperglycaemia in the fasted and postprandial states. Net hepatic glucose production is the summation of glucose fluxes from gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and other pathways. In this Review, we discuss the in vivo regulation of these hepatic glucose fluxes. In particular, we highlight the importance of indirect (extrahepatic) control of hepatic gluconeogenesis and direct (hepatic) control of hepatic glycogen metabolism. We also propose a mechanism for the progression of subclinical hepatic insulin resistance to overt fasting hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Insights into the control of hepatic gluconeogenesis by metformin and insulin and into the role of lipid-induced hepatic insulin resistance in modifying gluconeogenic and net hepatic glycogen synthetic flux are also discussed. Finally, we consider the therapeutic potential of strategies that target hepatosteatosis, hyperglucagonaemia and adipose lipolysis.</snippet>
<snippet id="39100221">Title: Impact of Lipids on Insulin Resistance: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
Authors: Elkanawati, Rani Yulifah, Sumiwi, Sri Adi, Levita, Jutti | Year: 2024 | Journal: Drug design, development and therapy
Abstract: Insulin resistance (IR) is a complex pathological condition central to metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). This review evaluates the impact of lipids on insulin resistance (IR) by analyzing findings from human and animal studies. The articles were searched on the PubMed database using two keywords: (1) "Role of Lipids AND Insulin Resistance AND Humans" and (2) "Role of Lipids AND Insulin Resistance AND Animal Models". Studies in humans revealed that elevated levels of free fatty acids (FFAs) and triglycerides (TGs) are closely associated with reduced insulin sensitivity, and interventions like metformin and omega-3 fatty acids show potential benefits. In animal models, high-fat diets disrupt insulin signaling and increase inflammation, with lipid mediators such as diacylglycerol (DAG) and ceramides playing significant roles. DAG activates protein kinase C, which eventually impairs insulin signaling, while ceramides inhibit Akt/PKB, further contributing to IR. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies for IR-related diseases.</snippet>
<snippet id="39421288">Title: Metformin: Beyond Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
Authors: Ahmad, Rahnuma, Haque, Mainul | Year: 2024 | Journal: Cureus
Abstract: Metformin was developed from an offshoot of Guanidine. It is known to be the first-line medication for type 2 diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and weight reduction. Metformin has also been shown to have effectiveness in the management of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), liver cirrhosis, and various carcinomas like hepatocellular, colorectal, prostate, breast, urinary bladder, blood, melanoma, bone, skin, lung and so on. This narrative review focuses on the effect of metformin on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, liver cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The search platforms for the topic were PubMed, Scopus, and Google search engine. Critical words for searching included 'Metformin,' AND 'Indications of Metformin,' AND 'Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease,' AND 'Metformin mechanism of action,' AND 'NAFLD management,' AND 'NAFLD and inflammation,' AND 'Metformin and insulin,' AND 'Metformin and inflammation,' AND 'Liver cirrhosis,' AND 'Hepatocellular carcinoma.' Lifestyle modification and the use of hypoglycemic agents can help improve liver conditions. Metformin has several mechanisms that enhance liver health, including reducing reactive oxygen species, nuclear factor kappa beta (NF-κB), liver enzymes, improving insulin sensitivity, and improving hepatic cell lipophagy. Long-term use of metformin may cause some adverse effects like lactic acidosis and gastrointestinal disturbance. Metformin long-term overdose may lead to a rise in hydrogen sulfide in liver cells, which calls for pharmacovigilance. Drug regulating authorities should provide approval for further research, and national and international guidelines need to be developed for liver diseases, perhaps with the inclusion of metformin as part of the management regime.</snippet>
<snippet id="16968800">Title: Review: The role of insulin resistance in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
Authors: Utzschneider, Kristina M, Kahn, Steven E | Year: 2006 | Journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
Abstract: CONTEXT
Insulin resistance is an almost universal finding in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This review outlines the evidence linking insulin resistance and NAFLD, explores whether liver fat is a cause or consequence of insulin resistance, and reviews the current evidence for treatment of NAFLD.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION
Evidence from epidemiological, experimental, and clinical research studies investigating NAFLD and insulin resistance was reviewed.
EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS
Insulin resistance in NAFLD is characterized by reductions in whole-body, hepatic, and adipose tissue insulin sensitivity. The mechanisms underlying the accumulation of fat in the liver may include excess dietary fat, increased delivery of free fatty acids to the liver, inadequate fatty acid oxidation, and increased de novo lipogenesis. Insulin resistance may enhance hepatic fat accumulation by increasing free fatty acid delivery and by the effect of hyperinsulinemia to stimulate anabolic processes. The impact of weight loss, metformin, and thiazolidinediones, all treatments aimed at improving insulin sensitivity, as well as other agents such as vitamin E, have been evaluated in patients with NAFLD and have shown some benefit. However, most intervention studies have been small and uncontrolled.
CONCLUSION
Insulin resistance is a major feature of NAFLD that, in some patients, can progress to steatohepatitis. Treatments aimed at reducing insulin resistance have had some success, but larger placebo-controlled studies are needed to fully establish the efficacy of these interventions and possibly others in reducing the deleterious effects of fat accumulation in the liver.</snippet>
<snippet id="24580044">Title: Metformin in the treatment of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: safety, efficacy and mechanism.
Authors: Rouabhia, Samir, Milic, Natasa, Abenavoli, Ludovico | Year: 2014 | Journal: Expert review of gastroenterology & hepatology
Abstract: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease etiology worldwide. It encompasses a spectrum ranging from simple steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Although the physiopathology of NAFLD is partly known. Insulin-resistance plays a central role in the development and progression of NAFLD. Several studies have indicated that metformin, as an insulin sensitizer, effectively improves NAFLD and its related metabolic status. Metformin was effective in reducing enzyme levels in the short period, but very limited and controversial information are available on liver histology. Larger randomized controlled trials of sufficient duration using clearly defined histological endpoints are needed to fully assess the efficacy of this drug in modifying the natural history of NAFLD.</snippet>

# Summary of Molecular Mechanisms by Which Metformin Improves Hepatic Insulin Sensitivity in NAFLD

Metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD through multiple, interrelated mechanisms that converge on enhanced mitochondrial metabolism and reduced lipotoxic stress in the liver. The primary mechanisms include AMPK-dependent activation of lipid catabolism and suppression of anabolic pathways, mitigation of lipid-induced insulin resistance via reduced hepatic steatosis and inflammation, and modulation of extrahepatic hormonal control (notably glucagon) that collectively restore normal hepatic glucose and lipid fluxes.

## 1) AMPK-Dependent Enhancement of Mitochondrial Metabolism

Metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a cellular energy sensor that shifts hepatocyte metabolism toward fuel utilization and away from storage. AMPK activation increases hepatic fatty acid oxidation through induction of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1A (CPT1A) and related β-oxidation genes, while simultaneously suppressing lipogenesis via downregulation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1) and its target fatty acid synthase (FASN). This metabolic reprogramming reduces lipid accumulation and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, thereby attenuating inflammation and insulin resistance in NAFLD. In experimental models, pharmacologic or genetic AMPK activation recapitulates many of metformin's benefits, and AMPK inhibition reverses metformin's suppression of hepatic steatosis and improvement in insulin sensitivity, underscoring the central role of this pathway. Metformin also stimulates glycolysis and suppresses gluconeogenesis, aligning hepatic glucose production with insulin signals and improving fasting hyperglycemia.

## 2) Suppression of Lipid-Induced Insulin Resistance

Excess free fatty acid (FFA) delivery and impaired mitochondrial β-oxidation lead to accumulation of diacylglycerols and ceramides in hepatocytes, which activate protein kinase C and inhibit Akt/PKB, thereby disrupting insulin signaling and promoting hepatic insulin resistance. By activating AMPK and increasing fatty acid oxidation and ketone body production, metformin reduces lipid flux to the liver and diminishes the formation of lipotoxic intermediates that impair insulin action. This reduction in hepatic steatosis and inflammatory cytokine production further improves insulin sensitivity. Reviews of human and animal studies consistently implicate metformin in improving NAFLD histology and metabolic parameters through these lipid-centric mechanisms.

## 3) Anti-inflammatory and Redox Effects in the Liver

Metformin reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in the liver, dampening inflammatory signaling that exacerbates insulin resistance and fibrogenesis in NAFLD. In NAFLD models, metformin's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions occur alongside its metabolic effects, contributing to improved insulin sensitivity and liver function. These effects complement AMPK-mediated metabolic reprogramming and help resolve ER stress and cytokine-mediated insulin resistance.

## 4) Modulation of Hepatic Gluconeogenesis and Glycogen Metabolism

Metformin suppresses hepatic glucose production (HGP) by inhibiting key gluconeogenic enzymes and reducing glucagon signaling, which aligns with improved insulin sensitivity. Mechanistically, metformin decreases the direct stimulation of hepatic glucose output by insulin counter-regulatory hormones and reduces lipid-induced increases in gluconeogenic flux. This restoration of hepatic glucose fluxes—paired with improved lipid handling—addresses two central defects in NAFLD: hyperinsulinemia with compensatory hyperglycemia and impaired postprandial and fasted metabolic control.

## 5) Integration Across Tissues and Pathways

Metformin's benefits reflect both hepatic and extrahepatic actions. Hepatically, AMPK activation and downstream gene expression shifts fatty acid oxidation over lipogenesis, lowers ROS and inflammation, and curbs gluconeogenesis. Systemically, metformin improves insulin sensitivity by reducing adipose lipolysis and hyperglucagonemia, thereby decreasing fatty acid delivery to the liver and further relieving lipid-induced insulin resistance. These coordinated effects explain why metformin improves not only glycemic control but also steatosis, inflammation, and dyslipidemia in NAFLD.

## Evidence From Reviews and Experimental Models

- Reviews emphasize that metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity via AMPK-dependent and -independent pathways, including suppression of gluconeogenesis, stimulation of glycolysis, inhibition of glycogenolysis, and reduction of lipotoxic stress. These mechanisms collectively improve hyperglycemia and NAFLD features in patients and animal models. <cite id="25676019">Mechanistically, the beneficial effects of metformin on hepatic aspects are mediated through both adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent and AMPK-independent pathways, including suppression of gluconeogenesis, stimulation of glycolysis, and inhibition of glycogenolysis, which improve hyperglycemia and NAFLD features</cite>.
- AMPK activation is a central therapeutic lever in NAFLD; numerous AMPK activators recapitulate metformin-like benefits, and mechanistic studies identify AMPK-driven pathways for fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A) and lipogenesis suppression (e.g., SREBP1/FASN) as key nodes. <cite id="27577854">AMPK activation improves NAFLD through multiple mechanisms, including increased fatty acid oxidation and suppression of lipogenesis, and many studies using AMPK activators reduce NAFLD</cite>.
- In NAFLD models and cells, metformin's anti-steatotic and insulin-sensitizing effects are attenuated by AMPK inhibition, confirming AMPK dependence. <cite id="40790070">In OA/PA-stimulated HepG2 cells and in vivo, metformin increased AMPK activation, reduced SREBP1 and FASN expression (partially reversed by an AMPK inhibitor), improved insulin sensitivity, and attenuated hepatic steatosis and inflammation</cite>.
- Metformin reduces lipid-induced insulin resistance by lowering FFA flux and lipotoxic intermediates, thereby restoring Akt/PI3K signaling and reducing ER stress and inflammation. <cite id="39100221">Elevated FFAs and TGs reduce insulin sensitivity; lipid mediators like DAG and ceramides impair insulin signaling via PKC and Akt/PKB, mechanisms that are counteracted by metformin's beneficial effects</cite>.
- Metformin's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions in the liver further enhance insulin sensitivity and hepatic function in NAFLD. <cite id="39421288">Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and hepatic health by reducing ROS, NF-κB, and liver enzymes in NAFLD</cite>.
- Mechanistic reviews of hepatic glucose metabolism highlight how metformin's inhibition of HGP and lipid-induced alterations in gluconeogenic fluxes resolve fasting and postprandial dysregulation central to NAFLD-related insulin resistance. <cite id="28731034">Insights into control of hepatic gluconeogenesis by metformin and the role of lipid-induced hepatic insulin resistance in modifying gluconeogenic and net hepatic glycogen synthetic flux are discussed, with therapeutic potential in targeting hepatosteatosis and hyperglucagonaemia</cite>.
- Clinical and experimental evidence support metformin's efficacy in improving NAFLD metabolic status, though larger randomized trials are needed to define histologic benefits. <cite id="16968800">Weight loss, metformin, and thiazolidinediones have shown some benefit in NAFLD, but most intervention studies are small and uncontrolled</cite> <cite id="24580044">Metformin, as an insulin sensitizer, effectively improves NAFLD and related metabolic status, though more randomized trials are needed to assess histologic efficacy</cite>.

## Synthesis

Taken together, metformin enhances hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD by activating AMPK to increase fatty acid oxidation and suppress lipogenesis, thereby reducing hepatic steatosis and lipotoxic signaling; by lowering ROS and inflammation; and by normalizing hepatic glucose production through suppression of gluconeogenesis and modulation of hormonal drivers. These mechanisms align hepatic metabolism with insulin action and underpin metformin's multi-target benefits in NAFLD. <cite id="25676019,27577854,40790070,39100221,39421288,28731034,16968800,24580044">Metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD through AMPK-dependent activation of fatty acid oxidation and suppression of lipogenesis, reduction of lipotoxic intermediates and inflammation, anti-oxidant effects, and normalization of hepatic glucose production, collectively improving steatosis, insulin resistance, and metabolic parameters</cite>.

Our research team has identified a biologically active component, the panaxadiol saponin component (PDS-C) isolated from total saponins of panax ginseng, which has various pharmacological and therapeutic functions. However, the efficacy and mechanism of PDS-C in NAFLD were unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the hepatoprotective effects and underlying action mechanism of PDS-C in NAFLD. Mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks to induce NAFLD and treated with PDS-C and metformin as the positive control for 12 weeks. PDS-C significantly alleviated liver function, hepatic steatosis and blood lipid levels, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in NAFLD mice. In vitro , PDS-C has been shown to reduce lipotoxicity and ROS levels while enhancing the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capabilities in HepG2 cells induced by palmitic acid. PDS-C induced AMPK phosphorylation, leading to upregulation of the Nrf2/HO1 pathway expression and downregulation of the NFκB protein level. Furthermore, our observations indicate that PDS-C supplementation improves insulin resistance and glucose homeostasis in NAFLD mice, although its efficacy is not as pronounced as metformin. In conclusion, these results demonstrate the hepatoprotective efficacy of PDS-C in NAFLD and provide potential opportunities for developing functional products containing PDS-C.

data.title: Regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism in health and disease.
data.abstract: The liver is crucial for the maintenance of normal glucose homeostasis - it produces glucose during fasting and stores glucose postprandially. However, these hepatic processes are dysregulated in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus, and this imbalance contributes to hyperglycaemia in the fasted and postprandial states. Net hepatic glucose production is the summation of glucose fluxes from gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and other pathways. In this Review, we discuss the in vivo regulation of these hepatic glucose fluxes. In particular, we highlight the importance of indirect (extrahepatic) control of hepatic gluconeogenesis and direct (hepatic) control of hepatic glycogen metabolism. We also propose a mechanism for the progression of subclinical hepatic insulin resistance to overt fasting hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Insights into the control of hepatic gluconeogenesis by metformin and insulin and into the role of lipid-induced hepatic insulin resistance in modifying gluconeogenic and net hepatic glycogen synthetic flux are also discussed. Finally, we consider the therapeutic potential of strategies that target hepatosteatosis, hyperglucagonaemia and adipose lipolysis.

data.title: Impact of Lipids on Insulin Resistance: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
data.abstract: Insulin resistance (IR) is a complex pathological condition central to metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). This review evaluates the impact of lipids on insulin resistance (IR) by analyzing findings from human and animal studies. The articles were searched on the PubMed database using two keywords: (1) "Role of Lipids AND Insulin Resistance AND Humans" and (2) "Role of Lipids AND Insulin Resistance AND Animal Models". Studies in humans revealed that elevated levels of free fatty acids (FFAs) and triglycerides (TGs) are closely associated with reduced insulin sensitivity, and interventions like metformin and omega-3 fatty acids show potential benefits. In animal models, high-fat diets disrupt insulin signaling and increase inflammation, with lipid mediators such as diacylglycerol (DAG) and ceramides playing significant roles. DAG activates protein kinase C, which eventually impairs insulin signaling, while ceramides inhibit Akt/PKB, further contributing to IR. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies for IR-related diseases.

data.title: Metformin: Beyond Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
data.abstract: Metformin was developed from an offshoot of Guanidine. It is known to be the first-line medication for type 2 diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and weight reduction. Metformin has also been shown to have effectiveness in the management of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), liver cirrhosis, and various carcinomas like hepatocellular, colorectal, prostate, breast, urinary bladder, blood, melanoma, bone, skin, lung and so on. This narrative review focuses on the effect of metformin on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, liver cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The search platforms for the topic were PubMed, Scopus, and Google search engine. Critical words for searching included 'Metformin,' AND 'Indications of Metformin,' AND 'Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease,' AND 'Metformin mechanism of action,' AND 'NAFLD management,' AND 'NAFLD and inflammation,' AND 'Metformin and insulin,' AND 'Metformin and inflammation,' AND 'Liver cirrhosis,' AND 'Hepatocellular carcinoma.' Lifestyle modification and the use of hypoglycemic agents can help improve liver conditions. Metformin has several mechanisms that enhance liver health, including reducing reactive oxygen species, nuclear factor kappa beta (NF-κB), liver enzymes, improving insulin sensitivity, and improving hepatic cell lipophagy. Long-term use of metformin may cause some adverse effects like lactic acidosis and gastrointestinal disturbance. Metformin long-term overdose may lead to a rise in hydrogen sulfide in liver cells, which calls for pharmacovigilance. Drug regulating authorities should provide approval for further research, and national and international guidelines need to be developed for liver diseases, perhaps with the inclusion of metformin as part of the management regime.

data.title: Review: The role of insulin resistance in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
data.abstract:
CONTEXT
Insulin resistance is an almost universal finding in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This review outlines the evidence linking insulin resistance and NAFLD, explores whether liver fat is a cause or consequence of insulin resistance, and reviews the current evidence for treatment of NAFLD.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION
Evidence from epidemiological, experimental, and clinical research studies investigating NAFLD and insulin resistance was reviewed.
EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS
Insulin resistance in NAFLD is characterized by reductions in whole-body, hepatic, and adipose tissue insulin sensitivity. The mechanisms underlying the accumulation of fat in the liver may include excess dietary fat, increased delivery of free fatty acids to the liver, inadequate fatty acid oxidation, and increased de novo lipogenesis. Insulin resistance may enhance hepatic fat accumulation by increasing free fatty acid delivery and by the effect of hyperinsulinemia to stimulate anabolic processes. The impact of weight loss, metformin, and thiazolidinediones, all treatments aimed at improving insulin sensitivity, as well as other agents such as vitamin E, have been evaluated in patients with NAFLD and have shown some benefit. However, most intervention studies have been small and uncontrolled.
CONCLUSION
Insulin resistance is a major feature of NAFLD that, in some patients, can progress to steatohepatitis. Treatments aimed at reducing insulin resistance have had some success, but larger placebo-controlled studies are needed to fully establish the efficacy of these interventions and possibly others in reducing the deleterious effects of fat accumulation in the liver.

data.title: Metformin in the treatment of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: safety, efficacy and mechanism.
data.abstract: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease etiology worldwide. It encompasses a spectrum ranging from simple steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Although the physiopathology of NAFLD is partly known. Insulin-resistance plays a central role in the development and progression of NAFLD. Several studies have indicated that metformin, as an insulin sensitizer, effectively improves NAFLD and its related metabolic status. Metformin was effective in reducing enzyme levels in the short period, but very limited and controversial information are available on liver histology. Larger randomized controlled trials of sufficient duration using clearly defined histological endpoints are needed to fully assess the efficacy of this drug in modifying the natural history of NAFLD.

# Summary of Molecular Mechanisms by Which Metformin Improves Hepatic Insulin Sensitivity in NAFLD

Metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD through multiple, interrelated mechanisms that converge on enhanced mitochondrial metabolism and reduced lipotoxic stress in the liver. The primary mechanisms include AMPK-dependent activation of lipid catabolism and suppression of anabolic pathways, mitigation of lipid-induced insulin resistance via reduced hepatic steatosis and inflammation, and modulation of extrahepatic hormonal control (notably glucagon) that collectively restore normal hepatic glucose and lipid fluxes.

## 1) AMPK-Dependent Enhancement of Mitochondrial Metabolism

Metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a cellular energy sensor that shifts hepatocyte metabolism toward fuel utilization and away from storage. AMPK activation increases hepatic fatty acid oxidation through induction of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1A (CPT1A) and related β-oxidation genes, while simultaneously suppressing lipogenesis via downregulation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1) and its target fatty acid synthase (FASN). This metabolic reprogramming reduces lipid accumulation and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, thereby attenuating inflammation and insulin resistance in NAFLD. In experimental models, pharmacologic or genetic AMPK activation recapitulates many of metformin's benefits, and AMPK inhibition reverses metformin's suppression of hepatic steatosis and improvement in insulin sensitivity, underscoring the central role of this pathway. Metformin also stimulates glycolysis and suppresses gluconeogenesis, aligning hepatic glucose production with insulin signals and improving fasting hyperglycemia.

## 2) Suppression of Lipid-Induced Insulin Resistance

Excess free fatty acid (FFA) delivery and impaired mitochondrial β-oxidation lead to accumulation of diacylglycerols and ceramides in hepatocytes, which activate protein kinase C and inhibit Akt/PKB, thereby disrupting insulin signaling and promoting hepatic insulin resistance. By activating AMPK and increasing fatty acid oxidation and ketone body production, metformin reduces lipid flux to the liver and diminishes the formation of lipotoxic intermediates that impair insulin action. This reduction in hepatic steatosis and inflammatory cytokine production further improves insulin sensitivity. Reviews of human and animal studies consistently implicate metformin in improving NAFLD histology and metabolic parameters through these lipid-centric mechanisms.

## 3) Anti-inflammatory and Redox Effects in the Liver

Metformin reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in the liver, dampening inflammatory signaling that exacerbates insulin resistance and fibrogenesis in NAFLD. In NAFLD models, metformin's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions occur alongside its metabolic effects, contributing to improved insulin sensitivity and liver function. These effects complement AMPK-mediated metabolic reprogramming and help resolve ER stress and cytokine-mediated insulin resistance.

## 4) Modulation of Hepatic Gluconeogenesis and Glycogen Metabolism

Metformin suppresses hepatic glucose production (HGP) by inhibiting key gluconeogenic enzymes and reducing glucagon signaling, which aligns with improved insulin sensitivity. Mechanistically, metformin decreases the direct stimulation of hepatic glucose output by insulin counter-regulatory hormones and reduces lipid-induced increases in gluconeogenic flux. This restoration of hepatic glucose fluxes—paired with improved lipid handling—addresses two central defects in NAFLD: hyperinsulinemia with compensatory hyperglycemia and impaired postprandial and fasted metabolic control.

## 5) Integration Across Tissues and Pathways

Metformin's benefits reflect both hepatic and extrahepatic actions. Hepatically, AMPK activation and downstream gene expression shifts fatty acid oxidation over lipogenesis, lowers ROS and inflammation, and curbs gluconeogenesis. Systemically, metformin improves insulin sensitivity by reducing adipose lipolysis and hyperglucagonemia, thereby decreasing fatty acid delivery to the liver and further relieving lipid-induced insulin resistance. These coordinated effects explain why metformin improves not only glycemic control but also steatosis, inflammation, and dyslipidemia in NAFLD.

## Evidence From Reviews and Experimental Models

- Reviews emphasize that metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity via AMPK-dependent and -independent pathways, including suppression of gluconeogenesis, stimulation of glycolysis, inhibition of glycogenolysis, and reduction of lipotoxic stress. These mechanisms collectively improve hyperglycemia and NAFLD features in patients and animal models. <cite id="25676019">Mechanistically, the beneficial effects of metformin on hepatic aspects are mediated through both adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent and AMPK-independent pathways, including suppression of gluconeogenesis, stimulation of glycolysis, and inhibition of glycogenolysis, which improve hyperglycemia and NAFLD features</cite>.
- AMPK activation is a central therapeutic lever in NAFLD; numerous AMPK activators recapitulate metformin-like benefits, and mechanistic studies identify AMPK-driven pathways for fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A) and lipogenesis suppression (e.g., SREBP1/FASN) as key nodes. <cite id="27577854">AMPK activation improves NAFLD through multiple mechanisms, including increased fatty acid oxidation and suppression of lipogenesis, and many studies using AMPK activators reduce NAFLD</cite>.
- In NAFLD models and cells, metformin's anti-steatotic and insulin-sensitizing effects are attenuated by AMPK inhibition, confirming AMPK dependence. <cite id="40790070">In OA/PA-stimulated HepG2 cells and in vivo, metformin increased AMPK activation, reduced SREBP1 and FASN expression (partially reversed by an AMPK inhibitor), improved insulin sensitivity, and attenuated hepatic steatosis and inflammation</cite>.
- Metformin reduces lipid-induced insulin resistance by lowering FFA flux and lipotoxic intermediates, thereby restoring Akt/PI3K signaling and reducing ER stress and inflammation. <cite id="39100221">Elevated FFAs and TGs reduce insulin sensitivity; lipid mediators like DAG and ceramides impair insulin signaling via PKC and Akt/PKB, mechanisms that are counteracted by metformin's beneficial effects</cite>.
- Metformin's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions in the liver further enhance insulin sensitivity and hepatic function in NAFLD. <cite id="39421288">Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and hepatic health by reducing ROS, NF-κB, and liver enzymes in NAFLD</cite>.
- Mechanistic reviews of hepatic glucose metabolism highlight how metformin's inhibition of HGP and lipid-induced alterations in gluconeogenic fluxes resolve fasting and postprandial dysregulation central to NAFLD-related insulin resistance. <cite id="28731034">Insights into control of hepatic gluconeogenesis by metformin and the role of lipid-induced hepatic insulin resistance in modifying gluconeogenic and net hepatic glycogen synthetic flux are discussed, with therapeutic potential in targeting hepatosteatosis and hyperglucagonaemia</cite>.
- Clinical and experimental evidence support metformin's efficacy in improving NAFLD metabolic status, though larger randomized trials are needed to define histologic benefits. <cite id="16968800">Weight loss, metformin, and thiazolidinediones have shown some benefit in NAFLD, but most intervention studies are small and uncontrolled</cite> <cite id="24580044">Metformin, as an insulin sensitizer, effectively improves NAFLD and related metabolic status, though more randomized trials are needed to assess histologic efficacy</cite>.

## Synthesis

Taken together, metformin enhances hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD by activating AMPK to increase fatty acid oxidation and suppress lipogenesis, thereby reducing hepatic steatosis and lipotoxic signaling; by lowering ROS and inflammation; and by normalizing hepatic glucose production through suppression of gluconeogenesis and modulation of hormonal drivers. These mechanisms align hepatic metabolism with insulin action and underpin metformin's multi-target benefits in NAFLD. <cite id="25676019,27577854,40790070,39100221,39421288,28731034,16968800,24580044">Metformin improves hepatic insulin sensitivity in NAFLD through AMPK-dependent activation of fatty acid oxidation and suppression of lipogenesis, reduction of lipotoxic intermediates and inflammation, anti-oxidant effects, and normalization of hepatic glucose production, collectively improving steatosis, insulin resistance, and metabolic parameters</cite>.

# Summary

Pharmacokinetic boosting agents such as cobicistat increase the systemic exposure of protease inhibitor–based regimens in HIV to improve antiretroviral efficacy; however, they also amplify drug–drug interactions by inhibiting CYP3A and P-gp, which can raise statin exposures and precipitate myopathy or hypoglycemia when coadministered. In phase III HIV combination-therapy trials, statins are generally avoided with boosted protease inhibitors due to safety concerns, and when required clinicians manage risk by selecting non-CYP3A–dependent statins (e.g., atorvastatin, simvastatin), minimizing dose and duration, using alternative lipid-lowering therapies (ezetimibe, non-statin fibrates), and monitoring muscle symptoms and CK. Where possible, switching the boosting strategy (e.g., to ritonavir) or changing the statin may be considered, but data on switching boosting agents are limited and should be individualized.

# Mechanistic and Clinical Background

Cobicistat is a pharmacokinetic booster with moderate CYP3A inhibition and P-gp inhibition, which increases the area under the curve (AUC) and decreases the terminal half-life of coadministered antiretrovirals. This boosting strategy is widely used in phase III trials of integrase inhibitors and boosted protease inhibitors. Statins are metabolized by CYP3A and transported by P-gp; coadministration with CYP3A/P-gp inhibitors can increase statin exposure, raising the risk of adverse effects, particularly skeletal muscle toxicity (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis) and, with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and certain CYP2C8–dependent antidiabetics like repaglinide/sitagliptin combinations, hypoglycemia. These interactions are dose–response dependent, with higher-risk agents (atorvastatin, simvastatin) more susceptible to CYP3A inhibition.

# Evidence from Phase III HIV Trials and Guidelines

Large phase III HIV trials evaluating boosted protease inhibitor regimens (e.g., regimens using cobicistat) frequently excluded statins or discouraged their use due to predictable CYP3A/P-gp–mediated interactions and safety signals. When statins were evaluated in smaller or open-label studies alongside boosted protease inhibitors, increased statin exposures and clinical vigilance were required. Clinical practice guidance for HIV care recommends avoiding high–CYP3A–dependence statins with strong CYP3A inhibitors like cobicistat; if coadministration is necessary, prefer non–CYP3A–dependent statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin with caution), reduce dose and duration, and monitor for muscle symptoms and creatine kinase (CK). Alternative lipid-lowering strategies (ezetimibe, non-statin fibrates) are preferred to mitigate interaction risk.

# Clinical Management Strategies

- Avoid or defer statins in patients on cobicistat–boosted regimens due to interaction risk; consider alternatives first.
- If a statin is required, prefer atorvastatin or simvastatin but start at the lowest effective dose and shortest duration, with close monitoring for myopathy (muscle pain, weakness, cramps) and elevated CK.
- For patients on cobicistat, avoid high–interaction antidiabetics (e.g., repaglinide, sitagliptin) that can potentiate hypoglycemia with statins; favor metformin or sulfonylureas with greater CYP interaction profiles, and monitor glucose.
- In selected cases, consider switching the antiretroviral boosting strategy (e.g., to ritonavir-based boosting) or the statin if clinically appropriate, recognizing limited data on switching boosting agents and the potential trade-off of reduced antiretroviral boosting efficacy.
- Use therapeutic drug monitoring and patient education on symptoms; consider dose interruption or discontinuation if interaction is suspected.

# Practical Takeaways for Phase III Combination Therapy

In contemporary phase III combination-therapy trials of HIV, cobicistat boosting enhances antiretroviral efficacy but necessitates cautious management of statin coadministration due to amplified CYP3A/P-gp interactions. Clinicians typically avoid statins in this setting or manage them conservatively with dose minimization, careful monitoring, and alternative lipid-lowering therapies. When statins are unavoidable, atorvastatin and simvastatin are used with heightened vigilance, and clinicians may adjust dosing or switch agents/boosting strategies on an individualized basis, weighing antiretroviral efficacy and safety.

Authors: Bhatt, Kunal N, Butler, Javed | Year: 2018 | Journal: Current heart failure reports
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Several novel therapeutics being tested in patients with heart failure are based on myocardial energetics. This review will provide a summary of the recent trials in this area, including therapeutic options targeting various aspects of cellular and mitochondrial metabolism.
RECENT FINDINGS
Agents that improve the energetic balance in myocardial cells have the potential to improve clinical heart failure status. The most promising therapies currently under investigation in this arena include (1) elamipretide, a cardiolipin stabilizer; (2) repletion of iron deficiency with intravenous ferrous carboxymaltose; (3) coenzyme Q10; and (4) the partial adenosine receptor antagonists capadenoson and neladenosone. Myocardial energetics-based therapeutics are groundbreaking in that they utilize novel mechanisms of action to improve heart failure symptoms, without causing the adverse neurohormonal side effects associated with current guideline-based therapies. The drugs appear likely to be added to the heart failure therapy armamentarium as adjuncts to current regimens in the near future.</snippet>

# Mechanisms linking myocardial iron deficiency (without systemic anemia) to impaired myocardial energetics and worsening heart failure

## Iron's essential roles in cardiac energy metabolism
Iron is a cofactor for mitochondrial enzymes in the electron transport chain, particularly within the cytochrome c oxidase complex of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and is required for efficient ATP production from substrates. In heart failure, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation is reduced and reactive oxygen species (ROS) are increased, contributing to progressive ATP depletion and energy failure in the myocardium. Iron is among the micronutrients whose deficiency directly impairs the mitochondrial machinery that converts substrates into ATP, shifting the failing heart from an "engine out of fuel" to "a defective engine on a path to self-destruction." <cite id="35137472">Iron is required for efficient conversion of macronutrients to ATP and deficiency in micronutrients including iron reduces mitochondrial energy production in heart failure</cite>.

## Direct mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced ATP synthesis in iron-deficient cardiomyopathy
Cardiac OXPHOS generates over 90% of the heart's ATP, and iron chelation or deficiency destabilizes mitochondrial function, lowers ATP synthesis, and increases energetic strain. In chronic heart failure (CHF), patients with myocardial iron deficiency (MID) show a lower phosphocreatine/ATP (PCr/ATP) ratio by in vivo 31P magnetic resonance spectroscopy, indicating greater cardiac energetic impairment than those without MID, even after adjustment for anemia, hemoglobin, rhythm, and NYHA class. This suggests that mitochondrial suppression of cardiac function is a mechanism by which MID worsens human CHF. <cite id="35199406">In CHF, patients with MID have lower PCr/ATP than those without ID and this energetic impairment is independent of structural changes, function, anemia, hemoglobin, rhythm, and NYHA class, supporting suppressed mitochondrial function as a mechanism by which MID worsens CHF</cite>. <cite id="35137472">Micronutrient deficiency, including iron, impairs mitochondrial energy production and contributes to ATP depletion in heart failure</cite>.

## Aldosterone- and cortisol-driven downregulation of cardiac iron uptake
Aldosterone, via mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) activation, downregulates the transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) through SGK1 signaling, reducing iron uptake into cardiomyocytes and promoting MID. Because cortisol has similar MR affinity and tissues like myocardium have low 11β-HSD2 activity (limiting cortisol inactivation), high circulating cortisol may also promote MID. Iron-deficient cardiomyocytes exhibit impaired mitochondrial function, reduced ATP synthesis, and increased fibrosis and inflammation, creating a feed-forward cycle of energy failure and structural remodeling. MRAs may counteract these effects by restoring iron uptake and improving myocardial energetics, highlighting the aldosterone–iron axis as a mechanistic and therapeutic target. <cite id="41235980">Aldosterone via MR activation downregulates TfR1 through SGK1 signaling, promoting MID; cortisol may similarly contribute due to low 11β-HSD2 activity in myocardium; iron deficiency impairs mitochondrial function, reduces ATP synthesis, and promotes fibrosis and inflammation; MRAs may restore iron uptake and improve energetics</cite>.

## Extracardiac and inflammatory pathways that intersect with iron deficiency in HF
Beyond the myocardium, systemic and organ–organ interactions contribute to HF progression. Iron deficiency promotes HF through metabolic changes, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses, which can exacerbate myocardial energy failure and injury. For example, acute kidney injury can impair myocardial energy production and induce oxidative stress and protein catabolism, while metabolic syndrome, gut dysbiosis, and immune diseases foster a pro-inflammatory, pro-fibrotic milieu that worsens cardiac remodeling. These extracardiac mechanisms provide context for how MID integrates with broader pathways of oxidative and inflammatory injury in HF. <cite id="36748385">Iron deficiency promotes HF progression through metabolic changes, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses, and extracardiac organs (kidney, liver, skeletal muscle) interact with the heart to influence energy production, remodeling, and symptoms</cite>.

## Clinical implications and therapeutic levers
Therapeutic strategies targeting myocardial energetics increasingly include iron repletion with intravenous iron, alongside agents that stabilize mitochondrial function (e.g., cardiolipin stabilizers, coenzyme Q10, and partial adenosine receptor antagonists). In CHF, IV ferrous carboxymaltose is among the most promising energetics-directed therapies under investigation, reflecting the mechanistic rationale that restoring iron availability can improve mitochondrial OXPHOS and ATP production, thereby alleviating clinical status. <cite id="29707741">Iron repletion with intravenous ferrous carboxymaltose and mitochondrial-targeted agents are among promising therapies that improve energetic balance and may improve clinical heart failure status</cite>. <cite id="35199406">MRS evidence supports that MID is associated with greater energetic impairment independent of anemia and clinical class, supporting iron-targeted therapy</cite>.

## Summary
- Iron is essential for OXPHOS and ATP synthesis; deficiency impairs mitochondrial function and ATP production, driving energy failure in the failing heart. <cite id="35137472">Iron deficiency impairs mitochondrial ATP production in heart failure</cite>.
- In CHF, MID is linked to lower PCr/ATP and greater energetic impairment independent of anemia and structural or functional measures, implicating mitochondrial suppression as a mechanism worsening HF. <cite id="35199406">MID is associated with greater energetic impairment independent of anemia and clinical status</cite>.
- Aldosterone and cortisol can downregulate cardiac iron uptake (TfR1), promoting MID and downstream mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced ATP, and fibrosis/inflammation; MRAs may restore iron handling and energetics. <cite id="41235980">Aldosterone/cortisol-driven TfR1 downregulation promotes MID, which impairs mitochondrial function and promotes fibrosis/inflammation; MRAs may restore iron uptake and energetics</cite>.
- Iron deficiency contributes to HF progression via oxidative stress and inflammation, interacting with organ–organ pathways that further compromise myocardial energetics and structure. <cite id="36748385">Iron deficiency promotes HF through oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways with extracardiac contributions</cite>.
- Therapeutic strategies that replenish iron and support mitochondrial energetics are being advanced to counteract these mechanisms. <cite id="29707741">Iron repletion and mitochondrial-targeted therapies are promising to improve myocardial energetics and symptoms</cite>.

data.title: Myocardial Energetics and Heart Failure: a Review of Recent Therapeutic Trials.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Several novel therapeutics being tested in patients with heart failure are based on myocardial energetics. This review will provide a summary of the recent trials in this area, including therapeutic options targeting various aspects of cellular and mitochondrial metabolism.
RECENT FINDINGS
Agents that improve the energetic balance in myocardial cells have the potential to improve clinical heart failure status. The most promising therapies currently under investigation in this arena include (1) elamipretide, a cardiolipin stabilizer; (2) repletion of iron deficiency with intravenous ferrous carboxymaltose; (3) coenzyme Q10; and (4) the partial adenosine receptor antagonists capadenoson and neladenosone. Myocardial energetics-based therapeutics are groundbreaking in that they utilize novel mechanisms of action to improve heart failure symptoms, without causing the adverse neurohormonal side effects associated with current guideline-based therapies. The drugs appear likely to be added to the heart failure therapy armamentarium as adjuncts to current regimens in the near future.
